#7707. Block, Blunt, Break: NATO’s New Theory of Victory

On October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s new theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. SACEUR’s speech comes at a time of considerable consternation in Eastern European capitals after months of suspected Russian hybrid activities including drone incursions and sabotage. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.

Block, Blunt, Break

General Grynkewich said that a classified version of this new NATO strategy had been agreed on by all 32 members of the Alliance about three months before his October 12 speech.[REF] He explained his decision to present Block, Blunt, Break in public as a helpful measure to assuage increasingly anxious NATO populations vulnerable to evolving security threats.[REF] General Grynkewich summarized his theory of victory as follows: “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”[REF]

Block. NATO land forces will meet any enemy assault with preponderant force at the point of contact and not trade territory for time. As these forces prevent adversaries from seizing Alliance territory, air and sea forces will gain superiority before aggressively supporting NATO forces on the ground. Space and cyber forces will be employed, creating a lattice of forces meant to prevent the enemy from holding its ground.

Blunt. Following the block phase, NATO forces will focus on denying the enemy’s ability to generate offensive momentum. This effort will include expanded deployments of manned and autonomous forces across domains to maintain operational advantage. The mass employment of effects in the forward battlespace will overwhelm enemy formations, thereby disrupting any continued advance.

Break. If the enemy continues its attack or employs reserves, NATO forces will expand operations to break the enemy’s broader warfighting system. NATO will apply mass pressure through all domains to break down the enemy’s ability to sustain its forces. A major contributing factor to this pressure campaign will be the pairing of precision munitions with sweeping volumes of attritable and affordable effects. These efforts will isolate enemy formations from replenishment and paralyze the command and control of the opposing force.[REF]

Strategic Context

This theory of victory is a marked shift from earlier NATO theories of victory, which focused on trading space for time—that is, allowing Russian forces to move into NATO territory, while NATO forces harass and slow Russian advances until decisive force can be brought to bear to destroy and then expel all Russian forces from NATO territory.

Block, Blunt, Break is a significant change from NATO Cold War strategy.

During the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.

Today, the Suwalki Gap between Lithuania and Poland is often cited as the modern equivalent of the Fulda Gap, especially because it separates Russian-allied Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.[REF] The three Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are for numerous reasons the NATO states against which full-scale Russian aggression is most likely; for example, Russian revanchists claim the existence of Russian-speaking minorities in Estonia and Latvia as a potential pretext, and Russian military planners could seek to connect the Russian exclave by land to either Belarus or Russia, and Lithuania is in their way. In the Baltic States, Block, Blunt, Break makes sense as the strategy for deterring or defending against Russian aggression from both a military planning and a political perspective.

From a military planning perspective, the lack of strategic depth in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania was likely a major factor in the change in strategy. Blocking the Russian advance from the outset prevents the Russians from gaining a foothold that may prove difficult to dislodge once fortified and reinforced.

From a political perspective, Block, Blunt, Break reinforces allied cohesion in the face of Russian aggression against a Baltic state or some other frontline state. Should Russia rapidly gain lodgment within Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, it could then sue for peace before NATO could dislodge Russian forces and liberate those three NATO members. This could well create real political divisions within the North Atlantic Council, in which some countries would press for the liberation of the Baltic States, while others may seek to accept the peace proposal. It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This new strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.

Strategic Signals

General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to demonstrate how NATO allies intend to prevent conflict and defeat aggression if needed. He stressed that NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy is defensive and seeks to prevent enemies from achieving their offensive objectives. While detailing this theory of victory, General Grynkewich provided a vision for a future NATO with enhanced military strength, operational readiness, and a unified commitment to the defense of all the Alliance’s territory.

This speech landed amid persistent suspected Russian gray-zone warfare against European NATO member states. On October 13, Bulgaria’s government summoned the Russian ambassador after two ships were hit by drones near its territorial waters.[REF] Two additional merchant ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria’s coast the week before, attacks that followed a strike on a civilian ship off Romania,[REF] and Romania has faced repeated Russian drone incursions over the past year.[REF]

While not mentioning these and other similar events directly, General Grynkewich stated that threats and intimidation against Alliance members will only bind NATO closer together. He noted that this unity is enhanced by the Alliance’s confidence in its ability to move up the escalation ladder if needed. General Grynkewich identified NATO’s strength, cohesion, and readiness as important factors that should significantly complicate an adversary’s military calculus of escalation. SACEUR also exhorted European NATO allies not to shy away from identifying the source of gray-zone provocations when they occur.

The United States’ ongoing European force posture review and discussions of a likely reduction in U.S. troop levels in Europe as part of the necessary rebalancing of forces to the Indo-Pacific have led to uncertainty among NATO allies regarding America’s contributions to the Alliance.[REF] General Grynkewich’s speech reaffirmed the United States’ commitment to European security, albeit within the larger framework of increased burden sharing promoted by the Trump Administration.

NATO’s theory of victory relies on aggressive, forward resistance to enemy advances. Implementing this operational concept will require the Alliance to bring substantial force to bear within a constrained timeline. While General Grynkewich’s speech serves as an overt commitment to a continued American presence in NATO, European states will likely have to shoulder a significant burden as part of the rapid joint response to an attack on the Alliance. To ensure NATO’s ability to execute this plan, European states should continue expanding their defense spending to improve their warfighting capabilities, forward-deploy certain capabilities, and substantially improve military mobility.

General Grynkewich prefaced his explanation of NATO’s theory of victory with a frank assessment of NATO’s security environment. He held that conflict is neither imminent nor inevitable. This status quo, he said, can be sustained by clearly articulating NATO’s intentions, maintaining open lines of communication with external states, and maintaining deterrence by denial through military capacity.

Commenting on the character of NATO, General Grynkewich stressed that the Alliance is defensive and has “no plans, no intentions, and no ambitions” other than the protection of NATO peoples and territories. SACEUR nevertheless cautioned potential adversaries not to mistake NATO’s defensive nature for a lack of resolve and emphasized that member states will ensure any attack on Alliance territory will prove futile.[REF]

This point was underlined by additional commentary regarding NATO’s deterrence posture. General Grynkewich drew attention to the Alliance’s “decision advantage.” He asserted that NATO will not be caught by surprise thanks to an immense intelligence footprint encompassing a vast network of sensors and sources. General Grynkewich framed NATO’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capability as a key enabler of the Alliance’s theory of victory. By rapidly assessing an opposing force’s presence and intent, NATO forces will have time to mobilize in the numbers required to deny attackers at the point of contact, especially because these troops will be reinforcing significant numbers of NATO troops forward positioned within NATO’s easternmost states.

Because of NATO’s doctrine, character, and posture, General Grynkewich remarked that the burden of escalation will always lie upon NATO’s aggressors. NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy seeks only to prevent an enemy from realizing its revisionist aspirations. He plainly asserted that such states will “bear the full moral, political, and strategic weight” of initiating and expanding conflict with the Alliance.[REF]

General Grynkewich included within this posture of deterrence and denial an explicit characterization of NATO’s intentions after the outbreak of conflict. He emphasized that the Alliance’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy does not seek at the outset to impose a strategic defeat upon its adversaries. Instead, NATO seeks simply to employ its theory of victory to maintain the Alliance’s territorial integrity by tactically defeating its attackers.

In sum, General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to communicate fundamental Alliance convictions to audiences both within and outside NATO. He articulated how NATO is not simply relying on decades-old defense strategies but adopting new means to meet emerging security threats. He delineated an internal Alliance dynamic defined by cohesion anchored in a collective determination to defend Alliance territory from opportunistic adversaries. He portrayed to external audiences a NATO whose mandate is limited to protecting its citizens and territory but that is also unified and firm in its willingness to fight and to defeat an aggressor if needed. General Grynkewich confidently messaged to Russia that he wants to assure those who “might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”[REF]

Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

#7706. This Supreme Court "Deserves Our Celebration, Not Our Condemnation"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Prof. William Baude on the Supreme Court and the false promise of court reform.

Professor William Baude has an op-ed in the New York Times, "This Is What an Independent, Competent Supreme Court Looks Like," defending the Supreme Court against its critics, left and right, and suggesting that many calls for court reform are misguided.

Noting that the Democratic electoral sweep has bolstered calls for reforming, and perhaps expanding, the Court to alter its course, Baude writes:

The left, understandably, strongly opposes the court's recent rulings on abortion, the Voting Rights Act, the unitary executive and so on. These decisions are a big deal. But court reformers still suffer from a failure of perspective. If Chief Justice John Roberts could write an opinion essay, I would imagine him saying: "What? Ruling against the administration's misuse of the National Guard, sweeping emergency tariffs and attack on birthright citizenship, plus preserving the independence of the Federal Reserve and the integrity of the midterm elections, wasn't enough for you?"

The court has ruled against the administration in high-stakes cases on those issues all in the past year. And it has done so even though six of the justices were appointed by members of the president's party — three by President Trump himself. . . .

Under the circumstances of the second Trump term, the Supreme Court is doing amazingly well. If anything, it deserves our celebration, not our condemnation.

Indeed, the Court's conservatives, on the whole, have shown themselves more willing to constrain Trump's excesses than were the Court's liberals when faced with executive branch overreach by Presidents Biden or Obama.

Baude notes that the Court's willingness to reject Trump Administration priorities has caused some on the Right to question the conservative legal movement's commitment to originalism, and cautions that "what goes around comes around, and principles will be worth more in the long run." Of course, some conservatives criticisms of the Court are for its failure to adhere to the principles some justices espouse, not that those principles are getting in the way of making America great again.

On the question of judicial reform, Baude strikes a cautionary note, particularly if court reform is nothing more than an effort to reverse the Court's current trajectory.

In the abstract, there is nothing wrong with bipartisan judicial reform. The Supreme Court should not be preserved in amber. But partisan judicial reform — reform motivated by frustration with specific judicial decisions and the hope that the reformed court will rule differently — is a dangerous game. Because partisan reform is a tactic equally available to both sides, it accomplishes little in the long run except to accelerate the court's transformation into a political superweapon. Such a tactic might be a short-run necessity in extreme circumstances, but we are far from those extremes.

He also--quite correctly--calls out the obsession with judicial ethics as "superficial." He could add that such concerns are nearly always one-sided and selective. While it may be appropriate to further limit the justices' outside income or ability to accept gifts, we should not pretend that any such reforms would have any effect on the Court's decisions.

The justices' views on big issues are well formed. The justices themselves aren't for sale; book income reflects their increasing celebrity, not any specific quid pro quo. To be sure, it is quite possible that travel and gifts and book sales subtly reinforce the justices' incentives to play to their respective fan bases. But this kind of corruption is quite indirect, and at the same time comes from so much more than money. So ethics reform is unlikely to change much about what the court actually does.

In the end, Baude thinks the best argument for court reform is as a placebo: To convince the public that something has been done so that attention can turn to more pressing issues. As he concludes this point: "If pointless reforms cause many Americans to believe that the court is better — more independent, less corrupt and so on — that would be great for the country."

I largely agree with Baude's piece, though I may be more open to certain sorts of reforms than he reveals in this piece. Reforms that represent genuine political engagement with the work of the courts, such as measures to alter or channel jurisdiction could be quite beneficial. Measures to reduce backlogs, limit forum shopping, constrain unwarranted or overly expansive equitable relief, and expand the Court's mandatory jurisdiction are all worth considering. They also represent the sort of meaningful legislation that Congress should engage in--legislation that requires Congress to take seriously its constitutional responsibilities. (In this regard, I view the willingness to engage with jurisdictional questions in the pending infrastructure reform bill to be a welcome sign, even if I might not endorse every jurisdictional measure the bill contains.)

As Baude ends his essay, courts are not above criticism, and this includes the Supreme Court. It is nonetheless is important to distinguish between criticisms of how the Court operates and performs its job from substantive or ideological disagreement with the decisions the Court reaches.

#7705. Gibson Dunn lands 120-lawyer group from Weil Gotshal, including firm’s co-managing partner

“This is the most sought-after ​cross-border funds team in the market, and their arrival is a ⁠defining moment for our practice,” said Shukie Grossman, the global chair of Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher’s investment funds ​practice, in a statement. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher has snagged a large part of soon-to-be defunct Weil, Gotshal & Manges, including its co-managing partner.

Reuters reported Thursday that Gibson Dunn has confirmed that it will bring aboard a 120-lawyer private funds group from Weil Gotshal, including co-managing partner Jonathon Soler.

According to Reuters, the group will include 23 partners across New York; Washington, D.C.; and London and is set to start at Gibson Dunn in January.

“This is the most sought-after ​cross-border funds team in the market, and their arrival is a ⁠defining moment for our practice,” said Shukie Grossman, the global chair of Gibson Dunn’s investment funds ​practice, in a statement.

The hires land days after Weil Gotshal’s partners voted earlier this week to wind down the 95-year-old law firm, a decision that followed an Oct. 28 recommendation from leadership.

According to Reuters, several firms have started, or are the in process of, absorbing groups of lawyers from the closing firm. Kirkland & Ellis said last week 40 lawyers will join, including private equity partner Ramona Nee, who had been in line to lead Weil Gotshal and was a co-managing partner alongside Soler.

Meanwhile, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom said Thursday it has hired three Weil Gotshal partners, adding to the two it picked up before the dissolution. Kirkland; Latham & Watkins; Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison; Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson; and Massumi + Consoli have also announced or confirmed Weil Gotshal partner hires this week.

Soler did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

#7704. John Yoo Joins the Exodus from California; Departs for Texas

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The University of California at Berkeley's law school loses its last right-leaning professor to teach in public law.

The Daily Californian reports that Professor John Yoo is leaving the University of California at Berkeley's law school. Beginning next year, he will be full-time at the University of Texas at Austin's School of Civic Leadership.

"Let the celebrations at my fan clubs in the City of Berkeley begin," Yoo said in an email. "Great as our university is, it would not allow a school to focus on restoring the central importance of western civilization to the education of all undergraduates." . . .

"I am sorry, however, that my departure will reduce the number of conservative professors in public law at Berkeley by 100 percent," Yoo said in the email. "I hope that the university will take this as an opportunity to consider that the notion of diversity should, most importantly, include ideology, not just the usual race, gender, and economic categories that my colleagues usually mean by diversity."

There had been one other right-leaning law professor at Berkeley, our co-blogger Orin Kerr, but he left Berkeley for Stanford in 2025.

According to Dean of Berkeley Law Erwin Chemerinsky, Yoo's decision to leave the faculty was entirely his own.

"John (Yoo) has been an important part of the faculty for many years," Chemerinsky said in an email. "This was entirely John's decision to retire. … He has indicated to me for a few years his thoughts about retiring. John is a very successful teacher and an eminent scholar." . . .

Yoo's move is also less drastic than it might appear, as he is moving from one blue state to another.  All of the other California transplants that have moved to Austin helped make sure of that (with a major assist from the Republican Party).

Harvard Law School suspended at least 18 students’ library access for two weeks after they participated in a “study-in” supporting clinical instructors earlier in November.

#7697. Judge releases DUI suspect after reading AI-assisted police report disclosure

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock)

An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

Anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

Court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

The officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”

Fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

Skiles of the FBI Miami Field Office. “The FBI remains committed to investigating human trafficking and working with our law enforcement partners to bring those who exploit others to justice.”

#7693. Breaking news: a new James Bond has been chosen!

The new James Bond has been announced!! Finally, after five years of waiting (since Daniel Craig departed the franchise with/in 2021’s sentimental No Time to Die), we have a new 007.

There has been much, much speculation about who would be the new Bond—the eighth actor to play Bond (in a legitimate adaptation… go away, 1967’s Casino Royale), and the star of the twenty-sixth Bond film. Would it be Slow Horses‘s Jack Lowden? Perhaps Josh O’Connor or Callum Turner? What about a dark horse, like CrimeReads favorite Josh Bowman? Remember way back when, when we all thought it would be Idris Elba? And remember how after that, we all thought it would be Aaron Taylor-Johnson?

Nope! Turns out, the next James Bond will be….

Yes, Robert Pattinson, the creative and hardworking English actor who will likely be nominated for a Supporting Actor Academy Award for his role as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, this year. Robert Pattinson! Robert Pattinson is Bond!

The Bond franchise has the power to catapult an actor from a lesser-known realm into wild international fame. As I wrote previously,

The individuals I refer to as the James Bond Selection Committee chose Daniel Craig last time; a well-respected actor of stage and screen, known mostly for supporting roles. The point of Bond casting is not to choose someone so closely associated with another leading man role that it becomes distracting; the actor must fully embody Bond.

This time, the selection committee chose Mr. Franchise, himself! Cedric Diggory of Harry Potter, Edward Cullen of Twilight (no matter how hard he tries to forget it), and Batman of The Batman! He’s about to be in Dune: Part III.

Pattinson, who is 40, has worked with countless extraordinary filmmakers in many challenging parts, distancing himself from the heartthrobby roles he played in his youth. He has already lead films directed by David Cronenberg, Claire Denis, Bong Joon Ho, Werner Herzog, the Safdie Brothers, Robert Eggers, James Gray, Lynne Ramsay, Christopher Nolan, Fernando Meirelles, and Denis Villeneuve (who will be directing the next Bond film).

Normally the James Bond persona subsumes the actor… the actor becomes Bond and always remains Bond, no matter what else he does. But Pattinson is so well-known already for his esoteric roles and big-budget blockbuster starring turns, and he himself has played so many famous characters, that this time (for the first time, I dare say), it’s the other way around.

Ben Roberts, the CEO of the British Film Institute (BFI), noted this, remarking, “He’s a different kind of choice… he comes to the table with a huge amount of baggage, adding that the “amazing thing about Robert Pattinson is his ability to be a chameleon in his roles.”

Personally, I think Pattinson is an extraordinarily skilled performer, one who manages to put a creative and memorable take on even the most generic or hard-worn characters. He’s certainly one of the best actors of his generation. I’m sure that he will be a fabulous Bond, even though I am admittedly surprised by the decision. Pattinson won’t let us down, that I know.

Well, this news also means that Matt Reeves’s sequel to his noirish 2022 masterpiece The Batman, titled The Batman: Part II, will probably be the end of that Batman series. I (and others) cannot imagine Pattinson doing a whole Batman performance in between James Bond performances. But… who knows? He’s a wild guy.

Still, Bond is a very demanding role. Just look at what poor Daniel Craig suffered through!

Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

Notably, however, this is the first James Bond film that will proceed without the famed Broccoli family/EON productions at the helm, ending their six-decade-long stewardship of the brand. In 2022, the tech giant Amazon acquired 50 percent control over the Bond property as part of its 2022 purchase of MGM (for $8.5 billion). Barbara Broccoli and her half-brother Michael G. Wilson, who inherited the rights from her father Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli upon his passing in 1996, had retained the other 50 percent, and had been guaranteed a final say on virtually everything. They had “ironclad creative control, deciding when to make a new Bond film, who should play the title role and whether remakes and television spinoffs got made” and “also had final say over every line of dialogue, every casting decision, every stunt sequence, every marketing tie-in, as well as every TV ad, poster and billboard.”

But in February 2025, after reported longstanding creative tensions between Barbara and Amazon, Barbara agreed to transfer creative control to Amazon. Wilson and Broccoli have chosen more passive roles. They will remain co-owners of the franchise, but are relinquishing all creative control to Amazon. In March 2025, it was announced that Harry Potter producer David Heyman would be in charge of the Bond property for Amazon, along with Amy Pascal. Their companies Heyday Films and Pascal Pictures, would produce the future Bond installments.

Almost nothing else is known about this next Bond film, except that the screenplay will be an original story (as there are no more of Ian Fleming’s Bond stories to adapt), written by Steven Knight, the creator of the series Peaky Blinders.

Stay tuned for more updates… and in the meantime, congratulations to Robert Pattinson! Cheers!

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

#7691. University of California law school offers intensive course on AI legal tool building

LexLab, the legal technology hub at the University of California College of the Law at San Francisco, is launching a three-day artificial intelligence legal tool building course, Law & AI Certificate Lab. (Photo by inkoly/Getty Images)

LexLab, the legal technology hub at the University of California College of the Law at San Francisco, is launching a three-day artificial intelligence legal tool building course, Law & AI Certificate Lab.

The intensive LAIC Lab course, offered Dec. 1-3, is a condensed, intensive version of one offered to law students over the course of a semester, offering lawyers and leaders a deep dive into the logic underlying legal AI while offering hands-on exploration of AI systems.

The course allows students to work with AI company Legora and AI platform Harvey as well as Replit, an app and website builder.

At the end of the certificate program, students should be able to move beyond using “chat” to build repeatable playbooks, checklists and other workflows; evaluate AI tools and vendors; determine whether tech should be bought or built; and manage privilege, confidentiality, conflicts and competence issues in AI-augmented practice.

#7690. Court appears unlikely to side with inmate in lawsuit for violation of his constitutional rights

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday appeared to side with a prison paramedic in a lawsuit brought by an inmate who contends that the paramedic’s failure to provide medical treatment violated his constitutional rights. During just over 80 minutes of oral argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, a majority of the justices seemed poised to throw out the inmate’s lawsuit, even if it wasn’t clear whether they were ready to bar such lawsuits more broadly in the future.

The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii. He says that he told Francis Nielsen, a paramedic who treated him, that his pain was severe, but he received only over-the-counter pain medication and was put in solitary detention, where he remained for more than two months without seeing a specialist or going to a hospital. When Watanabe received an X-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs. He relied on two Supreme Court cases: the court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, holding that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages; and its 1980 decision in Carlson v. Green, in which the court held that the estate of an inmate who died after having an asthma attack could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but explained that, in its view, “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Representing Nielsen, Lucas Walker told the justices on Monday that the Supreme Court “has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy.”

But Watanabe’s “claim ... also fails under a straightforward application of this Court’s Bivens framework,” Walker continued. “There are at least three” “meaningful difference[s] between his case and Carlson.” First, Watanabe had other options besides damages – such as seeking “administrative and injunctive relief.” Second, unlike the inmate in Carlson, Watanabe did not die, which “Congress could see [as] a meaningful difference.” Third and finally, there are “special factors” at play in Watanabe’s case that were not at play in Carlson, such as the Administrative Remedy Program, a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979, and federal laws enacted after the decision, such as the Prison Litigation Reform Act, a 1996 law that requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Vivek Suri, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the federal government, told the justices that, in the view of the United States, there are “three ways in which this Court could resolve the case.” “First, it could apply its existing standards and recognize that Carlson is now obsolete. Second, it could ... explicitly overrule Carlson. And, third, it could distinguish Carlson on its facts.” He “respectfully urge[d]” the court to choose one of the first two options, “either of which would abrogate Carlson, fully resolve the” divisions among the courts of appeals “that it has created, and end the severe practical problems that it creates for prison administration.”

Representing Watanabe, Joshua Wesneski reiterated that “the Court’s consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade” has been “[t]his far and no further.” “‘No further,’ he said, “means we should not extend those precedents. But ‘this far’ means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach.” “Indeed,” he suggested, “to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress’s measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society’s most vulnerable members.”

Neither Chief Justice John Roberts nor Justice Brett Kavanaugh seemed receptive to Walker’s suggestion that the court should go ahead and overrule both Bivens and Carlson.

Kavanaugh asked Walker how the court should handle the “fact ... that Congress has had 55 years since Bivens and 46 years since Carlson to do so and has not done so?” “It seems,” Kavanaugh continued, “like Congress, in fact, has left Bivens and Carlson where they stood ... and Congress has operated against that backdrop.”

Walker suggested that the Supreme Court “has not hesitated to overrule past decisions, especially those where the courts had overstepped the proper judicial role.”

In response to Walker’s assertion that overruling Bivens would “clear up the confusion and hand the accountability for all of this back to Congress, where it belongs,” Kavanaugh later asked whether “another way to provide clarity [would be] to simply say that courts should apply Bivens and Carlson but not extend them?” He compared such a scenario to what the Supreme Court has done in other areas of the law, such as with the Alien Tort Statute, “where we’ve had results or decisions under a methodology we wouldn’t use anymore, but we have not overruled the original three” causes of action under “the ATS, for example. We just haven’t extended them.”

Suri addressed this point during his time at the lectern, telling Kavanaugh that “[t]he problem ... as I see it ... is the Court’s decision” holding that “the PLRA itself gives rise to a new context,” as does “the availability of injunctive relief.” “So,” he continued, “if you’re going to honor that precedent, then this is a new context,” which would mean that “there are no viable Carlson claims anymore.”

For his part, Roberts noted that the federal government had “expressly” not asked the court to overrule Bivens, “and, of course, they have broad experience in this context. And I wonder,” he asked Walker, “if you have any insight into why or at least why shouldn’t we, on that question, defer to their expertise and experience on that question?”

Walker responded that “I think the answer is that this has been an area wrought with confusion where the lower courts have really called out for guidance.”

Roberts appeared unconvinced. “[O]n the other hand,” he countered, “it could be viewed as a cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question” to leave Bivens intact for now.

Several justices focused on whether, if a Carlson claim was not available, an inmate in Watanabe’s shoes would still have some remedy available to him. Justice Neil Gorsuch explored whether an inmate who was the victim of medical malpractice would still be able to obtain relief in a lawsuit against the United States (rather than the individual prison official) under Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 law that allows private citizens to sue the federal government for (among other things) injuries caused by a federal employee.

Gorsuch elicited from Suri that “[i]n almost all the cases that” he had “encountered, ... there is an FTCA claim brought in parallel” with the claim under Carlson – in part, Suri suggested, because the standard for prevailing is lower, qualified immunity does not apply, and “[y]ou have a defendant who’s able to pay, the United States.” Suri suggested that when an inmate does not bring both kinds of claims, it may be out of a desire to harass an individual prison official or because the inmates do not have lawyers and are instead representing themselves “and are confused about how to proceed. If this Court says there are no more Carlson claims,” he concluded, “then I think it’s more likely that they will bring FTCA claims in these cases.”

Justice Samuel Alito had a similar question, asking Suri “whether Bivens in this context provides anything ... of value that is not available based on other remedies.”

Suri responded that Carlson had rested on the idea that “the FTCA was insufficient” because it “does not provide for punitive damages.” In Bivens, he emphasized, the court faced a choice between “damages or nothing” for the plaintiff. But under the FTCA, he said, “you’re already getting damages.”

Wesneski pushed back on any suggestion that the FTCA, standing alone, would – as Kavanaugh put it – “provide some remedy in meritorious cases.” And there would be other potential problems as well, he posited: for example, he said, “we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA” under Indiana law.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett also expressed concern about what relief an inmate in a situation like Watanabe’s would be able to obtain. She first pressed Walker on the question of whether an inmate could obtain a court order instructing a prison official to do (or to refrain from doing) something, even if he could not obtain money damages for the official’s past conduct. “I want to make sure,” she said to Walker, “that, in your position, there’s no doubt that someone in a prisoner’s position like this would be able to get injunctive relief against a federal officer.”

And she later returned to a similar topic, asking Walker to “walk me through what happens in a case where a prisoner dies as a result of medical negligence and let’s say really horrific medical negligence. What recourse,” she enquired, “does that prisoner have? Is it the FTCA?”

Walker assured Barrett that, even if Carlson were overruled, claims like the one she described would generally be allowed to go forward.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to be the most likely to side with Watanabe. Sotomayor contended that, “in the Westfall Act, Congress looked at Bivens and explicitly reserved those constitutional claims the Court had recognized” – specifically, “Bivens itself for unlawful entry ... without probable cause into private citizens’ homes when there was malfeasance in doing so, and in Carlson itself, which was a ... medical malpractice claim.”

Walker resisted Sotomayor’s characterization, telling Sotomayor that, “respectfully, I don’t think the Court has ever gone so far as to say that the Westfall Act ratified Bivens or Carlson. But what the Court has said is that it does not provide any reason to extend those cases further.”

Jackson seemed to regard Watanabe’s case as, “with respect to all major indicia of sameness,” identical to Carlson. “We have the same kind of alleged violation as in Carlson,” she told Walker. “We have the same constitutional right brought under the same legal framework by the same kind of defendant who’s housed in the same kind of federal institution.”

By contrast, Justice Elena Kagan suggested that, at the very least, Watanabe’s case involves “factual differences.” In addition to the fact that the inmate in Carlson died, she noted that “there was a view that the prison officials had actively contributed to the injury, and ... that the prison officials knew exactly what was happening while it was happening.” “[A] different way of saying the same thing,” she added a few minutes later, “is that this looks like a pretty standard medical malpractice case, bad but standard, where the factual circumstances in Carlson look like something a good deal more than that.”

A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7688. Why the American West Is the Perfect Setting for a Crime Novel

Before we can answer the question of why the American West is the perfect place for a crime story, we need to clarify what the American West is. This is necessary because there seems to be a great deal of confusion on the subject. You can see this in almost any man-on-the-street interview which quickly reveals that the average American’s understanding of geography is less a body of knowledge than it is a collection of strangely confident opinions. For instance, people who live where I do, in Nevada, might look at Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington and think, “You people are practically sharing a driveway.” Similarly, many people who live along the Eastern Seaboard believe that anything west of the Mississippi River qualifies as the West.

For purposes of crime fiction, I propose that the American West should be considered any place that meets all five of the following criteria:

(1) It’s a Place Where Nobody Can Hear You Scream

I’m not kidding. The West has a lot of empty space. In Tallahassee or Atlanta, if someone screams at 2:17 a.m., seventeen people call 911. In Nevada, there may not be another person within 47 miles. This is both atmospheric and convenient for murder. And for crime authors. The amount of open space is incomprehensible to people who live in tighter confines and where the horizon often consists of a strip mall, a water tower and a billboard advertising personal injury attorneys.

Now, don’t get me wrong. There are a lot of desolate areas out here. But while there might not be any humans within earshot of your scream, rest assured the coyotes, wolves, bears, and other high school mascots can hear you. When you scream in the West, be careful, lest you inadvertently ring the dinner bell for some other kind of serial killer.

(2) It’s a Place Where You Can Hide a Body Almost Anywhere

When human remains are discovered in urban areas, there’s a good chance they’ve haven’t been hidden for more than ten minutes. That’s because there’s no good place to dispose of them without being caught on someone’s cell phone video. If you hope to hide your victim, you have to have a space in grandma’s wall or have a large, airtight cooler. In the West, you have deserts and mountains, some with places where no human has ever left a track. You have canyons so vast that the chances of finding a body begin to depend more on plate tectonics than police work. You have ghost towns with mine shafts so deep that any body placed in one will have to be carbon-dated if and when it’s ever found.

(3) It’s a Place Where Everyone Has a Truck

This solves an enormous number of plot problems for western crime authors. Need to transport a body? Truck. Need to follow someone into the wilderness? Truck. Need your protagonist to spend three chapters driving while contemplating the meaning of life? Truck.

Why does everyone in the American West have a truck, you ask? Because daily life demands one. Just watch any of those YouTube channels featuring people who camp in places a normal vehicle could never get to. I’m convinced many of these YouTube campers are serial killers. Also, in a lot of places, there are so few people that everybody knows everybody, so any crime committed has to be hidden where the eyes of prying neighbors aren’t focused. To get there, you need a truck. Trust me.

(4) It’s a Place Where Everyone Owns a Gun

As a writer of crime fiction, this is particularly useful because you can eliminate several pages of explanation.

In the American West, there are more guns than there are people. Most people own multiple firearms, and children are introduced to them shortly after learning to walk. Sometimes earlier. You may argue the merits of this…until little Tommy uses that .22 you bought him to shoot the rattlesnake that’s about to bite his sister. If, some years later, Tommy turns that same rifle on a person, well, that’s the makings of a pretty good crime story.

(5) It’s Place That Gives Your Detective Something Beautiful to Look at While Brooding

And this is, perhaps, the most important thing. The West is practically a literary service.

Mountain ranges. Sunsets. Deserts. Snow. Big sky. Canyons.

A detective in the West is never more than a few minutes away from something worth staring at while contemplating a murder, a missing person, a regrettable decision or the general decline of civilization.

Try doing that on the Jersey Turnpike. A detective there walks outside, looks dramatically into the distance and sees a Wawa.

The West gives a crime novelist something even more than just scenery: space. Space for a crime to happen. Space for a secret to survive. Space for a suspect to disappear. Space for a sheriff to chase him. And, most importantly, space for a character to stand on a ridge at sunset and wonder what the hell happened to his life.

For me, geography is everything. It’s as much a character in my novels as my protagonist, Porter Beck. When I build an outline for a new story, I plot the scenery just as I do my character biographies. I plot the time of year, the colors, the smells, the flora and fauna. In some cases – most actually – the physical setting is as much an adversary to Beck as the person he’s trying to stop. It might be snow drifts or wildfires or the relentless summer heat.

It’s the opportunities this landscape provides that make the American West the perfect place to stage a crime novel. Out here, there is room for everything a crime story needs.

BRUCE BORGOS lives and writes from the Nevada desert where he works hard every day to prove his high school guidance counselor had good instincts when he said “You’ll never be an astronaut.” He has a degree in political science which mostly served to dissuade him from a career in law while at the same time tormenting his wife with endless questions about how telephones work. When not writing, you can usually find him at the local wine store. He is the author of The Bitter Past.

#7687. Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

A Book Review of Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country (2026)”

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s new book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court. In his book, Justice Alito shares his thoughts about such subjects as originalism, textualism in statutory interpretation, the Catholic intellectual tradition, the role of judges in the United States and increasingly around the world, religious liberty in the United States, threats to the Constitution, and much more. Although there is a great deal else to be said, several things leapt out at me.

First, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned. Hence his vote to overrule Roe v. Wade after 49 years, Humphrey’s Executor after 91 years, or even a 128-year-old, long settled Supreme Court precedent like United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which would have ended birthright citizenship. (In saying this, I take no position myself on the birthright citizenship case – a debate I stayed out of.)

But Justice Alito is not simply an originalist. He also rejects the view of Professor James Bradley Thayer, and of Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Felix Frankfurter, William H. Rehnquist, and even at times of Justice Scalia that the Supreme Court should be judicially restrained and defer blindly to the political process. Justice Alito recognizes that judicial restraint where the Supreme Court has wrongly deferred to the political process is unconstitutional under Article III and has produced tragic results in cases like Plessy v. Ferguson, in which the court ratified Jim Crow race discrimination by the political branches of the government, or Korematsu v. United States, in which the court ratified President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s internment of over 100,000 innocent Japanese American citizens. In those cases the Supreme Court erred by not enforcing the Constitution. Yet at other times it has erred by being judicially activist as in Dred Scott v. Sanford or Lochner v. New York or Roe v. Wade. As Justice Alito teaches us, the Supreme Court should be neither judicially activist nor judicially restrained. It should uphold constitutional laws and strike down unconstitutional laws. This is what the rule of law is all about.

Justice Alito is equally and rightly skeptical of the notion that judges should be Dworkinian natural rights theorists, progressive constitutionalists like Chief Justice Earl Warren, or implementers of Catholic natural law as is argued by Harvard Law School Professor Adrian Vermeule. Indeed, Justice Alito devotes a whole chapter of his book to rejecting the idea that Supreme Court justices should implement natural law. This is because Justice Alito is profoundly aware that the American people during the 237 years from 1789 to 2026 have more knowledge and are thus wiser than is one individual Supreme Court, Supreme Court justice, or academic theorist. Although he does not say this outright, Alito appears to believe that originalist judges should be guided by the four cardinal virtues: 1) practical wisdom; 2) justice; 3) courage; and 4) temperance.

At the same time, Justice Alito is very much a Burkean. What does this mean? It calls to mind one of my favorite works of political philosophy, Friedrich Hayek’s volumes 1, 2, and 3 of Law, Legislation, and Liberty. In that masterpiece, Hayek identifies two forms of social order: planned systems of order like a firm or a military platoon, and spontaneous systems of social order like a language, the free market, or a culture of following the rule of law. No one has ever successfully planned a language, but languages have rules of grammar and a fixed meaning of words, and so a language forms what Hayek calls a spontaneous system of social order.

The Constitution and its amendments are a planned system of order, the words of which are so short and abstract that they have given rise to spontaneous systems of order around them. Thus, the freedom of speech and of the press protects thoughts in a private diary or a letter to a friend even though they are not vocal utterances or made with a printing press. Those words also protect freedom of expression in new technologies like movies, radio, television, or the internet, and they even protect expressive conduct that is not vocal at all like burning the American flag contemptuously at a protest rally.

The advantage of a spontaneous system of order like a language, the free market, or constitutional caselaw is that it harnesses the wisdom of many individuals who are always wiser than is one judge or academic theorist. But the countervailing advantage of the Constitution being a planned system of order is that if constitutional case law drifts too far away from the wonderful Novus Ordo Seclorum plan of the framers, the Supreme Court may overrule such caselaw – even after a century of it having been decided. The bottom line is that in figuring out when to follow the planned order of the Constitution or the spontaneous order of constitutional case law and precedents, a justice must further draw on the four cardinal virtues mentioned earlier – practical wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance.

More controversially, Alito argues that one factor in a good constitutional or statutory interpretation is that it produces good consequences. This is contrary to what Justice Scalia used to tell me when I was his law clerk, which is that if a text he is interpreting coming in is garbage, then the decision going out will also be garbage. Justice Scalia insisted it was not his job to make the law better. This differed from the approach which Judge Robert H. Bork, who I clerked for on the D.C. Circuit, followed. Judge Bork would not rewrite the Constitution or statutes to produce good results, but if there were two equally plausible readings of legal language, Judge Bork, like Justice Alito, would go with the one that produced the best outcomes in his view. I would do the same thing.

Nevertheless, in discussing Supreme Court precedents that he thinks were wrongly decided, Justice Alito can sometimes be too timid (in my opinion) in his criticisms. Perhaps that is because as a Supreme Court justice, he feels constrained in calling for the overruling of clearly incorrect precedents. For example, he criticizes Justice Scalia’s opinion in 2012’s United States v. Jones, in which the court held evidence should be suppressed which was obtained from illegally placing a GPS tracking device on a drug dealer’s car. But in his own dissent in that case Justice Alito failed to call for overruling the exclusionary rule cases on which that decision was based, even though his former boss, Attorney General Ed Meese, had publicly called for the overruling of the exclusionary rule in the 1980’s, and even though Congress passed a federal statute overruling it in the context of Miranda v. Arizona in 1968.

Justice Alito also complains rightly about the banning of religion from the public square, but he concedes in his book that as a justice he had failed to join a Scalia dissent, which called for the complete overruling of Flast v. Cohen, an absurd standing precedent of the Warren court which gave taxpayer standing to ACLU litigants who were offended by local government Christmas and Hannukah displays or displays of the Ten Commandments. And Justice Alito quite rightly criticizes Justice Scalia’s decision weakening the free exercise clause case in Employment Division v. Smith, but he does not call for overruling it. He should do so with pride.

The argument for originalism in constitutional interpretation is the same as the argument Justice Alito makes for textualism in statutory interpretation. Legal texts, be they constitutions, statutes, contracts, wills, or Supreme Court opinions should be given their original public meaning. A judge who interpreted a Supreme Court opinion or a contract according to natural law would be violating the fundamental norms of our legal system. Originalist justices can and should follow non-originalist precedents where not doing so would be disruptive to our legal system. I thus agree with Justice Alito that the Supreme Court should follow, for example, its dormant commerce clause precedents.

There is one final area where I and Justice Alito respectfully disagree. Readers of this site, and of Justice Alito’s book, know that we have different views on same-sex marriage and Obergefell v. Hodges. In his book, Justice Alito responds to me by pointing out, among other things, that same-sex marriage was unheard of for 40,000 years of human history.

I will only add here that 250 years ago, on July 4, 1776, nearly every country in the world had slavery, feudalism was widely practiced, there was a caste system in India, racism and religious persecutions were the norm, women’s rights were suppressed, and the public was adamantly opposed to LGTBQ+ rights. Gordon Wood, the famous historian of the American Founding argued in his Pulitzer Prize winning book, The Radicalism of the American Revolution that July 4, 1776 was the most important day in all of human history (other than the days of the birth and death of Jesus) because the Declaration of Independence launched a “New Order of the Ages,” which helped bring millennia of human inequality to an end in Western democracies.

It is true that same-sex civil marriage is a very new idea, but so too, in the historical scale of things, is the end or attempted end of slavery, feudalism, the Hindu caste system, racism, religious persecution, and sexism. I think the sudden rise of same-sex marriage stems from the same American Revolution that began 250 years ago on July 4, 1776.

In any event, Justice Alito is to be commended for writing an exceptionally intellectual and provocative new book. The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

#7686. Texas-Based Company Pleads Guilty to Trafficking Deadly Synthetic Opioids

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A business-to-business online marketplace headquartered in Texas — eWorldTrade LLC — pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute synthetic opioids for unlawful importation into the United States and agreed to pay a criminal fine of $1,350,000 based on its ability to pay.

“The Criminal Division will hold businesses accountable that facilitate the distribution of deadly drugs that put the lives of Americans at risk – just like we would any other drug dealer,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “These incredibly dangerous, illegal synthetic opioids were manufactured abroad but brought into the U.S. because of eWorldTrade. Companies who knowingly facilitate the illicit sale of controlled substances will pay the price for the Americans they put in harm’s way.”

“Businesses that knowingly facilitate the online sale of synthetic opioids are no less dangerous than cartels and foreign terrorist organizations,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Michael Perez of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Nashville. “Through close coordination with our law enforcement partners domestically and abroad, HSI will continue to identify and disrupt those networks.”

According to court documents, from March 2024 through March 2025, eWorldTrade offered registered users access to dozens of products through its website, including synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, carfentanil, and nitazenes. EWorldTrade knew that these products would reach the United States through its sales. Through its paid membership tiers, eWorldTrade offered customers easier access to premium suppliers of illegal drugs if they paid more to eWorldTrade, including to China-based sellers that openly offered and sold synthetic opioids through its website. The defendant admitted that its agents knowingly and intentionally facilitated prolific sales of these illicit controlled substances and others, including heroin and methamphetamine, from international sellers to potential buyers in the United States.

The Justice Department reached its resolution with eWorldTrade based on several factors, including the nature and seriousness of the offense. As part of the plea, eWorldTrade has agreed to enhance its compliance and internal controls and report to the Justice Department on remediation and implementation of the compliance measures throughout the term. EWorldTrade did not make a timely and voluntary disclosure of wrongdoing, but it received credit for its acceptance of responsibility and cooperation with the investigation, including collecting, analyzing, and producing voluminous information, providing timely updates on facts learned during its internal investigation, and engaging in timely remedial measures. The court will sentence eWorldTrade on Dec. 14.

The HSI Knoxville Office and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service’s Chattanooga Office investigated the case.

Trial Attorneys Jayce Born and Max J. Goldman of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF) are prosecuting the case.

MNF’s mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

MNF’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Unit investigates and prosecutes the top command and control elements of international drug cartels, drug trafficking organizations, and related transnational criminal organizations.

Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 67, of Michoacán, Mexico, a career drug trafficker for several Mexican cartels, was sentenced today to 270 months in prison for international drug trafficking and firearm offenses.

Wenshen Xu, 52, a Honduras-based Chinese national extradited from Guatemala, was sentenced today to 12 years in prison, five years of supervised release, and a $22 million money judgement for...

Donelfert Monterroso Vasquez, 51, a Guatemalan national, pleaded guilty today to conspiring to import more than 450 kilograms of cocaine into the United States.

#7685. Rhys Bowen on writing real people and settings in historical fiction

One of the aspects of the Royal Spyness series that readers like is that it involves the British royal family in the 1930s. The Prince of Wales, Mrs. Simpson the king and queen, the little princesses walk across the pages and are part of the plots. Other well-known real characters also are featured: Coco Chanel in a couple of books, Noel Coward in several and even Agatha Christie helps solve a mystery in From Cradle to Grave. My fictional heroine is supposedly related to the royals, a great granddaughter of Queen Victoria and thus a cousin first cousin once removed to the Prince of Wales.

Introducing real people to my plots is a bit of a risk, I suppose, but I am by no means unique. Shakespeare certainly wrote about plenty of real people but he retold their true lives. Taking a real person and putting them into a fictional plot is a little different. It is stretching truth and not everybody will be happy with that.

When I started the series I had to think how far I wanted to go from what we know of these characters and I decided I wanted to keep as close as possible to what I knew they said and felt. Queen Mary was a stickler for rules and passionate about antiques so in one plot I had her charge my heroine with reclaiming an antique that had been stolen from her.

I suppose the one person I took the most liberties with was Mrs. Simpson. Since I knew she had a sharp tongue and could be very cruel I enjoyed making her quite unpleasant for several books until she ends up helping my heroine.

Using real people and real settings requires a lot of research. I have to confess that I have poked into every corner of Buckingham Palace, and Kensington Palace, read all the biographies of Chanel and Noel Coward, the Prince of Wales and Mrs Simpson. To me it is important to recreate a real person as faithfully as possible.

In writing about real people each author has to decide how far they want to go and in what ways they might deviate from truth.  Some writers have taken real people and made them sleuths. Stephanie Baron made Jane Austen (very successfully) into a sleuth. Karen Harper had  Queen Elizabeth I solve crimes. Gyles Brandreth makes Oscar Wilde a detective.

Did any of these people really have time to do a little detecting on the side? And without being observed? Jane Austen clearly could have been a good sleuth with her powers of observation of the human condition, especially as she would have been overlooked, sitting in a corner as an unmarried woman. But Queen Elizabeth was accompanied every second of the day.  Could she have found time and opportunity to sleuth a little?

So is the writer allowed to take real people and make them do things they didn’t do? Is there a chance of getting sued? Apparently not if they were a public figure. I could include Agatha Christie in my book, doing what she did best…solve a crime. But I don’t know about making them do something they would never have done: make them a murderer? I think the family would have cause to bring a lawsuit if a respectable person was defamed.

I don’t think I would be comfortable with making a real person do things I know they didn’t do. In fact it gives me great pleasure in having real characters say things I knew they really said. It’s like weaving reality and fiction together.

My favorite example is when Lady Georgie meets her cousins Princess Elizabeth and Princess Margaret. Margaret is three at the time. Georgie says “Hello Margaret,” and Margaret replies, “You have to say Princess Margaret because I’m a princess.” To this Georgie says, “Then you have to say Lady Georgie to me because I’m a lady.”

Margaret looks up at her governess and asks, “Is a lady better than a princess?” To which her governess replies, “One hopes a princess will grow up to be a lady.” True story!

For me the appeal of using real characters and putting my fictional heroine into a real world is that it immediately gives her credibility. It justifies her existence. She’s moving through a real society so we now believe she is real. We know all about Edward VIII and Mrs Simpson and we see Lady Georgie interacting with them. So we accept Lady Georgie as real. Very satisfying.

As well as involving real people in my stories I have introduced real events. We were at Sandringham for the last days of King George V. We were with Mrs Simpson when the king decided to abdicate.

In this latest book in the Royal Spyness series, To Crown It All (book twenty!) the whole story centers around a real event: the coronation of King George and Queen Elizabeth in 1937. This was a well-documented event,  It was even filmed. So I made sure I kept every element completely accurate (except for a minor detail of a plot nobody knew about…which might have happened).

I reasoned that my heroine, Lady Georgie, who is the king’s cousin, would be invited to the Abbey and be involved in the coronation, but I didn’t expect her to get so very involved!

I find it very satisfying to recreate real history, to take readers back to a real time and place, but with the slight addition of my fictional sleuth.

Rhys Bowen is the New York Times bestselling author of more than sixty novels, including Mrs. Endicott’s Splendid Adventure, The Rose Arbor, The Paris Assignment, Where the Sky Begins, The Venice Sketchbook, Above the Bay of Angels, The Victory Garden, The Tuscan Child, and In Farleigh Field, the winner of the Lefty Award for Best Historical Mystery Novel and the Agatha Award for Best Historical Novel. Bowen’s work has won sixteen honors to date, including multiple Agatha, Anthony, and Macavity Awards. Her books have been translated into many languages, and she has fans around the world, including more than seventy thousand Facebook followers. A transplanted Brit, Bowen divides her time between California and Arizona. For more information, visit www.rhysbowen.com.

#7683. Immigration agents’ seizure of lawyer’s phone at airport appears retaliatory, judge finds

A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at a Boston airport in 2025. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal judge ruled Friday that it is likely that U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents were retaliating against an immigration attorney for criticizing federal immigration policies when they seized his cellphone at the Boston Logan International Airport in September 2025.

U.S. District Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the District of Massachusetts also found that federal agents likely violated the First Amendment rights of Andrew Lattarulo, a co-owner of the law firm Georges Cote in Massachusetts. Lattarulo runs an Instagram account featuring videos explaining immigrants’ rights and critiquing federal immigration policies.

After agents seized Lattarulo’s phone without a warrant and downloaded a copy of its contents, they returned the phone. The government has claimed that the seizure was part of an investigation into his firm for potentially employing unauthorized immigrants.

Lattarulo’s lawsuit alleges that agents targeted him because of his advocacy and seized information that included confidential communications with his clients.

Burroughs’ ruling mandates that federal officials preserve all copied cellphone data without accessing it as litigation continues, according to a story by Law.com.
