#7681. 7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

Means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction. Of the three features, I appreciate motive as the real heart of a mystery story.

For two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries. Prior to that, I was a psychology major and a social worker. I have always been fascinated by what makes people tick. While the success of a work of fiction in any genre may depend on the specifics, for me, its true value lies in the universal truths about human experience that it portrays and reveals. In Louise Penny’s words, “crime was deeply human.”

Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.

No one weaves a mystery from its three strands better than the grande dame of crime fiction, Agatha Christie. In Five Little Pigs, a young woman asks Hercule Poirot to investigate the death of her father for which her mother was convicted sixteen years earlier. The evidence at trial was overwhelming and the accused woman’s defense weak.

Shortly before her own death, the mother professed her innocence to her child in a letter. Due to the passage of time, Poirot must depend on character, rather than evidence, to solve the case. He says, “[Character] is the principal interest of all my cases.” The “five little pigs” are the five people, other than the wife, who had the opportunity to kill Amyas Crane, a talented but eminently unlikeable painter.

Initially, none of the five appears to have a motive to murder him. Poirot tells one of the suspects, “the reason for murder is nearly always to be found by a study of the person murdered.” As Poirot delves into the past, he uncovers the truth about Crane’s life and learns that each of the five did, indeed, have a motive. His analysis of the behavior and motivations of several of the suspects ultimately leads him to the solution.

More than sixty years after Christie’s novel was published, Louise Penny introduces another wise Francophone inspector, Armande Gamache. He, too, investigates the murder of an artist.

The puzzle in Still Life is that, unlike Christie’s victim, Jane Neal of the idyllic Quebecois village of Three Pines was beloved by all. When Neal’s body is found in the woods, felled by an arrow, on Thanksgiving morning, Gamage asks, “who would want to kill kindness?” He later explains “most premeditated murders were about rancid emotions, greed, jealousy, fear, all repressed.”

Penny introduces us to a host of Three Pines villagers, among whom are both suspects and others who will become fond recurring characters in future books, the twenty-first of which was just published this fall.

Sal, a lonely sixth-grade boy, discovers the burned body of middle-school teacher Adam Merkel in the Nevada desert. Merkel had befriended the traumatized boy who came to live on a nearby ranch with his reclusive uncles after the death of his mother.

When one of Adam’s colleagues, who is dealing with her own personal issues, takes it upon herself to investigate, she uncovers secrets in Adam’s past as she also senses that Sal knows more about Adam’s death than he will admit. Her consideration of possible motives explores how the past and present are immutably intertwined.

Sixteen-year-old Lydia Lee has gone missing. When her body is found in a local lake, her devastated parents need to know how and why it happened. Was it a drowning accident, suicide, or foul play?

While this moving novel is not a mystery in the traditional sense, it is an exquisite portrayal of how we are shaped by our families and our experiences and how our motives and actions arise from them. As the family’s emotions and secrets long held in silence are slowly and painfully brought to light, we learn the secrets that Lydia, her siblings, her parents, and their parents have harbored, which ultimately reveal Lydia’s fate.

This historical legal mystery is set in a small town in 1946 Mississippi. Pete Banning is an upright, church-going model citizen and World War II hero. After returning from the Philippines and the horrors of his war experience there, he hopes to resume the life he left behind with his wife Liza and their children on their cotton farm. When he has Liza committed to a psychiatric hospital and, soon after, calmly shoots his pastor and friend, Dexter Belland, Banning refuses to defend himself, stating only, “I have nothing to say.”

Inspired by an actual case from the 1930’s in which the defendant made the same statement until his execution, Grisham keeps the reader guessing until the end why Banning is prepared to die, rather than reveal his motive.

A murder mystery within a murder mystery. Editor Susan Ryeland receives the manuscript of her client, author Alan Conway’s latest mystery novel featuring detective Atticus Pund, but with the story’s ending missing.

When Conway is found dead, Ryeland concludes that the manuscript involves real-life events and that Conway’s murderer stole the final pages to avoid incrimination. Ryeland sets out to find the motive and perpetrator of Pund’s fictional mystery to find Conway’s real-life killer.

Stuart Turton, The 7 ½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle

Straddling genres, this mystery borrows from speculative fiction to shift time and perspective as the protagonist investigates a murder from the viewpoints of multiple characters within the setting of a classic English country estate. Aiden Bishop wakes up at Blackheath Manor with amnesia and no knowledge of why he is there.

In each of eight days in a time loop, he finds himself inhabiting a different guest at the manor until he can solve the murder of the young heiress of the estate, Evelyn Hardcastle, who died that evening. If he cannot solve the case by the end of day eight, he is doomed to repeat the cycle with his memory wiped clean.

Whatever the setting or sub-genre, the key to a murder mystery is motive. As Inspector Armande Gamage put it, “My job is to find people who take lives. And to do that, I have to find out why.”

Alice Openshaw has been a fan of mysteries since the age of ten, when she discovered Perry Mason books at her tiny town’s public library. She holds a BA in psychology from Middlebury College in Vermont and an MLS from Vanderbilt University. She lived in rural Maine for thirty years, where she worked as a librarian and adult literacy teacher and raised three children and an assortment of animals on a small farm. She now lives near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, with her husband and her tuxedo cat, Frankie. On the Killer's Trail is her debut novel.

#7680. Eleven new relists in search of four votes

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

First, some old business. The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser. After three relists, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown finally got the nod. The court will decide when bankruptcy courts can refuse to enforce arbitration agreements in suits alleging violations of the automatic stay. But two-time relist Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia struck out: The court denied without comment the petition brought by Roberto Clemente’s family over Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image, which raised questions about takings of intangible property and Puerto Rico’s sovereign immunity.

After a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 new relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week. Several come in pairs or trios, and the federal government – the court’s most successful repeat litigant – advocates review in three of them.

The government seeks asylum – from the D.C. Circuit

The most consequential new relist this week may be Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. On his first day back in office, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10888, which suspended the entry of aliens “engaged in the invasion across the southern border” and barred those who violate the suspension from invoking provisions of the immigration laws that would let them stay, including asylum.

Three nonprofits and 13 individuals sued. The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States. It held unlawful the proclamation’s restrictions on asylum and other statutory protections, as well as its authorization of removal procedures outside those established by Congress, and issued a classwide injunction. A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit narrowed the class definition, but affirmed. It reasoned that although asylum is discretionary, the executive cannot categorically deny covered migrants access to asylum by proclamation and informal guidance rather than through the procedures Congress prescribed. Judge Justin Walker dissented in relevant part.

The solicitor general’s petition argues that asylum is discretionary and that the president may categorically deny it to those covered by the proclamation. Requiring the government to accept applications it has already decided to reject, the government contends, serves no purpose. It also challenges the classwide injunction and the breadth of the certified class. The government argues that the ruling threatens to revive chaos at the border. Iowa and 21 other states support the petition, arguing that the decision undermines the federal duty to protect the states against invasion.

The respondents’ brief in opposition argues that Congress expressly gave noncitizens physically present in the United States the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered, and that the president cannot eliminate that right by proclamation. They emphasize the absence of a circuit split and dispute the government’s claims that the policy was responsible for reducing border crossings. They call the remedial issues fact-bound and say the government overstates the border crisis, noting that apprehensions had already fallen more than 90% from their peak before the proclamation.

The D.C. Circuit’s mandate is stayed, leaving the asylum restrictions in place for now. The absence of a split weighs against review, but the invalidation of a major administration policy could well persuade the justices to take another trip to the border. Will the court resolve this case quickly or let it sit for a while as it decides what to do, as it has in other high-profile cases?

Our first group of cases asks whether Washington may regulate private companies that run federal immigration detention centers. In GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, a class of detainees and the state sued GEO, which operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma under a federal contract, for not paying Washington’s minimum wage to detainees in a voluntary work program for which ICE reimburses $1 a day. GEO argues it’s not a conventional labor relationship, but just an effort to prevent the detainees from becoming restless from idleness. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit certified the question to the Washington Supreme Court, which held that the state minimum-wage law applied to the detained workers. A divided panel of the 9th Circuit then rejected GEO’s supremacy clause defenses, leaving GEO with a judgment it puts at about $37 million. Seven judges voted to rehear the case en banc, and six joined dissents, arguing that (among other things) the state law “interferes with federal immigration-detention policy” and thus directly regulates the federal government.

GEO argues that Washington cannot regulate a federal detention program through a contractor while exempting its own detainees from the wage law. Washington and the detainees respond that the law applies equally to every private detention contractor, whether it works for a city, the state or the federal government, and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit applies the same test as the 9th. The detainees also note that ICE has since revised its detention standards, which they say limits the decision’s future impact.

In a court-invited amicus brief, the U.S. solicitor general recommends granting review. The government argues that the law discriminates against the federal government, because Washington exempts its own facilities while barring itself from contracting with private ones, and that federal statutes leave detainee pay to the Secretary of Homeland Security. It also says the decision conflicts with a decision of the 3rd Circuit ruling on a New Jersey law targeting private detention contractors.

GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson challenges a 2023 Washington statute regulating private civil detention facilities, which GEO says reaches its Tacoma facility alone. The district court preliminarily enjoined it, but the 9th Circuit vacated that ruling, rejecting GEO’s direct regulation and preemption claims and remanding on its discrimination claim against private contractors. GEO says Washington is micromanaging federal detention by regulating a contractor; the state says its requirements resemble those governing other civil facilities. It also points to further proceedings on remand as a reason not to intervene yet.

A grant in Nwauzor seems likely; Ferguson presents a closer question, but at minimum it seems likely to be held if Nwauzor is granted.

Two companies that went public while business was booming present a question of required disclosures in federal securities filings: How much bad news must a company reveal? Two related relists ask the justices to clarify when withholding information makes an IPO registration statement misleading under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933.

In Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, the online brokerage rode the GameStop meme-stock frenzy and Dogecoin boom into its July 2021 IPO. Robinhood warned that trading might decline and provided an estimate of second-quarter revenue, but investors say it withheld information showing that trading and other business metrics were already declining. A district court dismissed their claims, but a divided panel of the 9th Circuit revived them. Robinhood’s petition argues that merely omitting material information cannot create liability unless the omission makes an affirmative statement misleading or violates a specific disclosure requirement. The investors respond that the company’s disclosures presented a misleading picture of its performance. The U.S. solicitor general, invited to weigh in, recommends granting review on the Section 11 misleading-omissions question, but not on a separate question concerning disclosures of known trends under Item 303 of Regulation S-K (which the agency is reviewing).

In ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, a webinar-platform provider prospered as businesses moved online during the pandemic. Investors allege that the company knew before the IPO that many pandemic-era customers did not intend to renew. An unpublished 9th Circuit memorandum revived the suit. ON24 asks whether describing an unmaterialized risk as hypothetical is misleading, alleging a split with the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd and 10th Circuits, and raises two questions that overlap with Robinhood’s. ON24 argues that the court improperly required it to predict future customer cancellations; the investors respond that “the warned-of risk was already materializing.” ON24 also asks the justices either to grant its petition or hold it for Robinhood. Leadersel Innotech answers that the 9th Circuit decision is non-precedential and that the panel found the risk had already begun to materialize.

With the solicitor general supporting review in Robinhood, a grant there looks plausible. Whether ON24 gets invited along is less certain. It seems a likelier hold.

It’s not every week that the Taliban is a respondent in the Supreme Court. That said, it has not responded, leaving an Afghan diplomat filing an amicus brief to oppose review – not on the Taliban’s behalf, but on behalf of the Afghan people.

When the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, the Treasury Department blocked billions of dollars that Da Afghanistan Bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Victims holding judgments against the Taliban sought to execute on the funds under Section 201(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which makes the blocked assets of a terrorist party and its “agency or instrumentality” subject to execution.

A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover. It held that an entity’s status as a terrorist organization’s instrumentality must be determined when its assets were blocked, before the Taliban installed its officials at the bank. Separately, the panel rejected other plaintiffs’ attempt at prejudgment attachment, holding that Da Afghanistan Bank enjoys sovereign immunity as the central bank of Afghanistan, which the executive continues to recognize as a foreign state. Judge Richard Sullivan dissented.

In Havlish v. The Taliban, judgment holders challenge the blocking-date rule, alleging a conflict between the 2nd Circuit and the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 9th and 11th Circuits. They are backed by Iowa and 30 other states.

In Owens v. The Taliban, plaintiffs who lacked judgments when the district court ruled say the 2nd Circuit is the first court of appeals to require courts to defer to the executive on “foreign state” status, and thus “breaks with th[e] consensus” positions of the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd, and 6th Circuits. Ashton v. The Taliban joins Owens in arguing that courts should not defer to the executive branch in determining whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, and seeks a GVR in light of this year’s decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A.

As noted, no respondent has appeared. The only opposition is an amicus brief jointly filed in the three cases by Naseer Faiq, chargé d’affaires of Afghanistan’s mission to the United Nations, who says no one is currently authorized to appear for Afghanistan in U.S. courts. He argues that the facts are unlikely to recur, that there is no circuit split, and that the immunity issue affects only the petitioners’ priority among creditors. The Havlish petitioners have sought leave to respond, arguing that the legal question is likely to recur in terrorism litigation and does indeed implicate a circuit split.

At the very least, the court will need more time to figure out what to do when the respondent seems unwilling to appear to defend the cases.

How many places can a state declare off-limits to firearms before the Second Amendment right to carry in public becomes largely theoretical? That’s the question in Novotny v. Moore, a challenge to Maryland’s extensive restrictions on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”

Maryland prohibits licensed gun owners from carrying firearms in numerous locations, including public transportation, parks and forests, healthcare facilities, museums, stadiums, casinos, public demonstrations, and establishments serving alcohol. I thought this was America! A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld those restrictions, finding historical support for them under the Supreme Court’s decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Judge G. Steven Agee dissented as to many of the restrictions, warning that the majority had stretched the sensitive-places exception too far. The panel separately struck down Maryland’s presumptive ban on carrying firearms on private property open to the public.(After this year’s decision in Wolford v. Lopez, which struck down Hawaii’s similar private-property rule, Maryland dropped its own cert petition seeking review of that ruling.)

The gun owners’ petition argues that historical restrictions on carrying firearms in sensitive places were generally limited to locations where the government provides security, not ordinary places where people gather. Maryland responds that historical regulations support restrictions at crowded places and locations serving vulnerable populations, and contends that review is unnecessary because the lower courts largely agree on the governing principles.

Invoking Wolford, the petitioners ask the justices to grant review or at least send the case back for reconsideration. Whether the court is ready to take on the sensitive-places doctrine so soon after Wolford remains to be seen. But reconsideration under Wolford seems like a real possibility.

In Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, the Commission fined Sprint $12.2 million and T-Mobile $80.1 million for failing to adequately safeguard customers’ location information shared with third-party aggregators, including by continuing to disclose the information after learning of significant security vulnerabilities. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the penalties, concluding that information about a cellphone’s location – even when no call is underway – qualifies as confidential “customer proprietary network information” under the Communications Act.

The carriers’ petition argues that the statute protects only call-location information, not all device-location data. They also contend that the FCC circumvented a statutory penalty cap by treating separate relationships with third-party companies as multiple “continuing violations,” and that the D.C. Circuit improperly deferred to the agency’s interpretation despite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. But the carriers’ principal request is narrower: They ask the justices to send the case back in light of this year’s decision in FCC v. AT&T, which held that an FCC forfeiture order does not itself compel payment. That opinion, the carriers say, rested on a key government concession: A company can refuse to pay and contest the penalty in a subsequent enforcement proceeding with a jury. Sprint and T-Mobile say they paid under protest because the FCC’s orders demanded payment and existing precedent left them little choice. The government responds that the carriers always had the option not to pay, that they failed to preserve their claim of being misled, and that AT&T provides no reason for reconsideration. The carriers disagree.

A remand remains possible, although the government notes that the court rejected a comparable request from Verizon. For now, Sprint and T-Mobile are hoping the justices will take their call.

How long can a “hot pursuit” stay hot after police lose sight of the suspect? That’s the question in City of North Las Vegas v. Jones, a case arising from a search for a suspected domestic abuser that ended with police entering a stranger’s backyard and shooting two dogs. The suspect was never found.

After officers saw a man flee over a backyard wall, the officers stated that they established a neighborhood perimeter rather than pursuing him on foot. A K-9 officer arrived about 18 minutes later, and during the ensuing search, his police dog alerted them toward a walled backyard. An officer climbed in without a warrant. Three pit bulls emerged, two of which attacked the police dog and were shot. The dogs’ owners, Genoa Jones and Cornell Tinsley, sued. The district court granted the officers qualified immunity, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed on the warrantless-entry claim, holding that the officers had not been in immediate and continuous pursuit and that circuit precedent clearly established the search’s illegality. It left intact qualified immunity for shooting the dogs. Eight judges dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc.

The city’s petition argues that the officers never abandoned the pursuit: They say they established a perimeter and used a police dog to locate a potentially dangerous suspect. Even if the search was unlawful, the city argues, no sufficiently specific precedent clearly established that fact. It also asks the justices to hold that only Supreme Court decisions – not lower-court precedent – can clearly establish law for qualified-immunity purposes. The homeowners respond that the officers never actually established a perimeter or chased the suspect and instead just conducted a neighborhood-wide search without knowing his whereabouts.

The eight dissenting judges may help keep the petition warm. But the court closely reviews many petitions in cases where police are denied qualified immunity, and unless the error was clear enough to warrant summary reversal, the justices may let this pursuit go cold – perhaps with a dissent from denial of cert.

The court has enough to chew on that it seems likely to take a while to finish processing this week’s new offerings. As for me, I’ll be watching Monday’s orders to find out how much of this I get to reuse.

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause allows a state to reclassify federal immigration detainees participating in a federal work program as employees and thereby impose its state minimum-wage law just because a private contractor provides detention services at the federal facility where the detainees are housed.

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by failing to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider material, without an inquiry into whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading; and (2) whether an issuer violates Item 303 – and thus Section 11(a)’s required-statements prong – by failing to disclose and quantify interim financial data before quarterly reporting deadlines.

Issue: Whether Maryland’s numerous prohibitions on carrying firearms in many places frequented by the general public violate the Second and 14th Amendments.

City of North Las Vegas, Nevada v. Jones, 25-1355

Issues: (1) Whether officers’ warrantless search of a backyard in close proximity to the domestic violence victim’s residence was a lawful “hot pursuit” when the suspect’s trail was temporarily lost within the perimeter for approximately 18 minutes but recovered through immediate and continuous police efforts; (2) whether, even if the search did not qualify as a “hot pursuit,” the officers were entitled to qualified immunity because no “clearly established law” was violated; and (3) whether, in the interest of avoiding the perpetual flood of federal court qualified immunity litigation, the court should decide that clearly established law means only the decisions of the Supreme Court, and not lower court decisions, which fail to provide police departments with meaningful guidance because they are highly fact-determinative and subject to numerous differing and often contradictory judicial interpretations.

ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, 25-1376

Issues: (1) Whether an issuer violates Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933’s misleading-omissions prong by describing unmaterialized risks as hypothetical; (2) whether an issuer violates Section 11(a)’s misleading-omissions prong whenever it omits information related to a disclosed fact regardless of whether the omission renders an affirmative statement misleading; and (3) whether an issuer violates Item 303 of Regulation S-K – and thus the prong of Section 11(a) prohibiting the omission of required statements – by failing to disclose immaterial facts as “known trends or uncertainties” that are reasonably likely to have a material impact on financial results.

Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, 25-1422

Issues: (1) Whether this court should grant, vacate, and remand in light of FCC v. AT&T, Inc. and the government’s concessions in that case; (2) whether “location” customer proprietary network information under 47 U.S.C. § 222 refers only to call-location information, not other formation about the location of a mobile device; and (3) whether the number of “continuing violations” arising from a single failure to act under 47 U.S.C. § 503(b) is a legal question for courts to decide, without deferring to the Federal Communications Commission’s conclusion.

Issue: Whether the supremacy clause permits a state to enact a law micromanaging the details of how a federal contractor must provide services at a federal detention facility, while exempting the state’s own detention facilities from all those requirements.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, 26-239

Issues: (1) Whether Presidential Proclamation No. 10888 and its implementing guidance – which suspended the entry of certain aliens and precluded their access to statutory provisions that would enable their continued presence in the country, including asylum – are lawful; (2) whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) bars the classwide relief entered by the district court; and (3) whether the class definition comports with Article III and Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

Issue: Whether, under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, a plaintiff’s right to execute on blocked assets depends on whether the assets’ owner was a terrorist party or its agency or instrumentality at the time the assets were blocked.

Issue: Whether, in light of the court’s intervening decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A., which confirms that a court – not the Executive Branch – must resolve through ordinary statutory construction whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, the judgment below should be vacated and remanded so that the Second Circuit must reconsider, under the correct framework, whether the Taliban and its instrumentalities are entitled to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act.

Issue: Whether the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act requires courts to independently interpret its provisions, or whether a court must defer to State Department websites and Department of Justice litigation filings in determining whether an entity is entitled to sovereign immunity under the FSIA.

Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes a government speech.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether, in a use-of-force case which involves multiple instances of force, Barnes v. Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, whether the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a violation of a clearly established constitutional right; and (2) whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a complete lack of training on the constitutional right in question.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25-1404

Issues: (1) Whether the harassers’ subjective discriminatory intent is an element of a hostile environment claim under Title VI; and (2) whether the First Amendment bars a plaintiff from pleading a Title VI hostile environment claim based on “protected speech.”

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the law clearly established that the officer’s use of a less-lethal projectile, under the totality of the circumstances, constituted an unreasonable use of force in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

(Relisted after the Oct. 9, Oct. 16, and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issue: Whether an automobile is per se an instrumentality of interstate commerce, which would make a federal offense of every kidnapping involving an automobile under 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1).

(Relisted after the Oct. 16 and Nov. 6 conferences.)

Issues:(1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

#7679. “Lows” Gang Member Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison For His Participation in a RICO Conspiracy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal judge sentenced Deontae Jackson, 37, of Minneapolis to 10 years in prison for his role in a Racketeering Influenced Corrupt Organization (RICO) conspiracy that included violence and fentanyl distribution. Jackson is the first of 14 defendants sentenced in this case, U.S. v. Alowonle et al. (24-cr-293).

According to court documents, beginning on or about 2009 and continuing through at least April 2026, Jackson was a member of and associated with the Lows gang. The Lows gang does not have a formal structure or initiation process as it is comprised of several affiliated subsets. Members would prove their loyalty by “putting in work,” which included committing acts of violence and drug trafficking.

Between February 2023 and May 2024, Jackson sold fentanyl as part of, and to benefit, the Lows gang. The Lows drug trafficking activities during this period involved over 1.2 kilograms of fentanyl.

On April 26, 2024, law enforcement searched a home in Fridley, Minnesota, where Jackson was staying. In Jackson’s bedroom, officers found approximately 945 M-30 fentanyl pills, which collectively weighed around 94.5 grams. At the time of the search, Jackson was on electronic court monitoring in connection with his conviction for a gang-related drive-by shooting. After the search, Jackson removed his ankle monitor to avoid having his location tracked.

In May 2024, law enforcement tracked Jackson to Bismarck, North Dakota. Officers then searched Jackson’s hotel room where he was staying with a fellow Lows member and two others. Police recovered a bag containing 2,599 M-30 fentanyl pills that weighed approximately 270.4 grams. In a second bag, officers found 20 more M-30 fentanyl pills that weighed 2.08 grams.

#7678. Catherine Townsend on treating dating like detective work, and vice versa

When I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work. I’d flag that in both scenarios, you find yourself sitting in front of a stranger—the difference being that in a potential love match, the skeletons in their closet are (hopefully) merely metaphorical, rather than decomposing in a crawl space.

The same logic works in reverse. Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date. The idea is to ask open-ended questions and to encourage the person you are trying to get information from to keep talking about themselves. If they keep talking, eventually you can find the inconsistencies in their story.

A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con. When we like someone, our brain is wired to look for commonalities. And the more we like someone, the more we mimic their behavior. This works extremely well for getting someone to trust you— and that is why con artists mimic our movements, too, for less pure reasons.

But my job when I’m conducting an interview is to see the worst in people.

In 2010, I was living in Los Angeles, had just enrolled in PI school with Dale, and was moonlighting as a PI. State boards give credit to-ward investigative hours for police work, which is why retired police detectives can qualify as licensed private investigators. But, despite the fact that investigative journalism uses a lot of the same skill sets as detective work, journalists are given zero credit for hours worked in newsrooms.

My first encounters with law enforcement had been less than satisfactory, and I was convinced that this was because, for the most part, they didn’t trust the media. So I wanted to get some more specialized training, something that would raise my skill levels and, hopefully, my esteem in the eyes of the police departments that I was trying to sweet-talk.

Living in Los Angeles, the quintessential sunny place for shady people, is like having permanent residence inside a noir mystery painted with the rainbow neon sunsets, and traffic jams, of Grand Theft Auto V.

Dale sent me out on a lot of matrimonial surveillances, and they almost always unfolded in the same way.

Sometimes, the clients would summon me to their homes. But, following the detective manual logic on interrogations, I preferred to coax the clients into nonthreatening, neutral territory—preferably one that invoked feelings of nostalgia. I found that magic location sliding into a red leatherette booth at Bob’s Big Boy diner in Burbank at sunrise, sipping a ten-ounce mug of Big Boy medium roast, and watching the pink clouds float across an impossibly bright, Monet-meets-vaporwave California sky.

After that, things usually get complicated. The client asks me to follow their boyfriend/husband/girlfriend/married boyfriend who also has another girlfriend but has promised that they are his only mistress. (I pretend to ignore the logical fallacies of that argument.) I ask them what they hope to accomplish from a surveillance.

I’m honest: I’ll tell them that it’s expensive, uncertain, and a hell of a lot harder than it looks on TV. (If you don’t believe me, try identifying a subject described as “white man in a suit” outside a downtown office building at night from a fuzzy Facebook photo. Bonus points if it’s a rainy winter night and only a few inches of skin are visible!)

I’ll also ask them why they believe that their loved one has been unfaithful, and often they will tell me something that lets me know that they already know the truth: Maybe they have found a topless selfie of his secretary, or a scrap of lacy women’s underwear in the glove compartment of his Prius.

I try to always have these conversations over something sweet, which is why I prefer to meet at restaurants. I load the table with strawberry waffles or a banana milkshake with extra maraschino cherries, since bad news goes down easier with a heavy dose of sugar lubricant. Even Cinnabon at the mall food court is better than nothing: Studies show that our animal brains associate the smells of cinnamon and vanilla with comfort and security.

“Well, it sounds like you already know the answer,” I inevitably say. Why would you think that this is a good person, despite mounting evidence to the contrary?

Before I dig in and disrupt lives, potentially unearthing a truth that could shake the foundations of a person’s existence, I always ask the same question: Do you really want to know? Little white lies can be the glue that holds relationships together. No, you don’t look fat in those white jeans. Yes, you’re the best sex I’ve ever had.

I make a point of sliding one of my Patrick Bateman-style thick business cards across the table and making a reference to The Matrix: Would they rather take the blue pill and remain blissfully ignorant, or the red pill to see where the rabbit hole, however unpleasant, leads?

Some people have a compulsive need to know the reality, however brutal and disruptive it will be to their existence, and they will continue to pick it apart like an overeager esthetician digging out blackheads on YouTube. And then there are those who decide that for whatever reason—long marriage, double mortgage, social hierarchy, or something else—they want to stay inside the much happier bubble they have created.

Before you ask a question that could shatter your reality forever, it’s important to know which camp you fall into. Because once the bubble is pierced, it’s almost impossible to get back in—and if a person chooses to overlook a betrayal, an infidelity, or something worse, lying to themselves afterward can become a full-time job.

Catherine Townsend is a journalist, private investigator, and podcaster. She is the host of the iHeartMedia podcast Hell and Gone and Red Collar. After beginning her career as a staff writer for New York Magazine, Catherine moved to London to create The Independent’s very popular “Sleeping Around” dating column. Her articles have appeared in publications including The Atlantic, Elle, New York, GQ, Marie Claire, Cosmopolitan, The Daily Mail, The New York Post, Investigation Discovery, and HuffPost. She became a licensed private investigator in 2013. She is the author of How to Survive a Murder Investigation: A True Story of Death and Danger in the Ozarks.

#7676. Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards showed a court open to the possibility of a major limitation on the ability of agencies to impose fines or penalties under internal adjudicative processes, at least without ready review in court.

The constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article II of the Constitution). The Supreme Court always has recognized that it is permissible for officials in the executive branch – who don’t have the protections (including life tenure) that Article III gives to federal judges – to resolve questions in a proceeding that looks an awful lot like the kind of trial you might see in a federal court. And it also on several occasions has invalidated schemes that seemed to the court to go too far in that direction. To pick the most famous example, the justices invalidated the initial version of the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 because it gave undue adjudicative responsibility to bankruptcy “judges” that are not protected by Article III. What the court has never done well is explain exactly how far such powers can go. Nevertheless, recent decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a great willingness to rein in the powers traditionally granted to the administrative state.

This case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States. Conventionally, when the Department of Labor decided that an employer had failed to treat workers as it promised pre-admission, it imposed fines or penalties in an administrative proceeding, often handing the funds over to the employees as compensation in the nature of back pay. The question for the justices is whether Article III of the Constitution can tolerate that dispute being resolved internally by DOL employees rather than by judges in a federal court.

The government sees the dispute as squarely involving two categories of so-called “public rights” for which Article I treatment is permitted: the immigration power and public benefits. The immigration power is involved because the workers were permitted to enter the country on the condition that the employer treat them as agreed; the public benefit power is involved because the right to enter is a benefit almost entirely within the discretion of the executive.

Several of the justices found that argument rather weak. Chief Justice John Roberts, for example, commented early on that the leading case about the immigration power (Oceanic Steam Navigation v Mellor) “had to do very much with entry, a condition of entry, and loathsome diseases. This strikes me as significantly different. … You’re trying to leverage an entry several weeks, months … in the past to the particular condition of work that doesn’t seem to have much to do with the actual entry.” For the chief justice, the government was trying to “leverage what is a significant barrier to entry, where you have a lot of deference to the executive branch,” and “trying to … extend that broad authority beyond the justification for its application.” He repeatedly emphasized that the specifics of the case “look more like a condition of employment rather than … entry.”

In a similar vein, Justice Amy Coney Barrett stated to Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris (arguing for the government): “I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our immigration tradition without an Article III court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different. …. So I’m … wondering here why that wouldn’t be the case for the alien. If the alien violated some sort of condition on the H-2A visa, why wouldn’t the alien be entitled to an Article III court before the alien had to pay that kind of a fine?” At which point Justice Neil Gorsuch chimed in that he “thought [an earlier case had said that] confiscating property goes to an Article III court when you’re trying to confiscate property from aliens. … I thought we decided a long time ago that you’ve got to go to an Article III court. Are … you resisting that?”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed to yet another precedent on civil penalties: “In Tull [v. United States], we said … and this is 40 years ago – a civil penalty was a type of remedy at common law that could only be enforced in courts of law. …. That’s a fairly definitive statement in our precedent. What … are we supposed to do with that?”

That’s not to say that all of the justices sided against the government. Justice Elena Kagan, for example, found the case well within the boundaries of existing doctrine. To Harris, she commented early on: “[I]sn’t there a condition of entry here? … [T]hey wouldn’t be admitted unless the employer had promised certain things.” To Robert Johnson arguing on behalf of the employer – a different Robert Johnson, not the blues singer – she was much more pointed:

Offering a parallel perspective, Ketanji Brown Jackson emphasized that the court in numerous contexts has approved administrative adjudication of civil penalties. She repeatedly challenged Johnson to reconcile his argument with those decisions.

But ominous for the government was some repeated questioning of Harris about “the best way for you to lose” (as Justice Sonia Sotomayor put it). From early on in the argument, even the justices who seem most likely to accept the constitutionality of the arrangement were trying to help Harris identify the least damaging way for the court to rule against her. At the beginning of her argument and throughout it, Harris emphasized to the justices that a broad ruling against her on the constitutional question would unsettle programs in a wide variety of areas, ranging from Medicare, to government contracts, to student loans, but that did not seem to make any headway for her.

It is not at all clear from the argument how exactly the justices are going to come down. Clearly a significant group are considering the idea that an award of civil penalties is too far removed from the entry of the employee to be protected by the “public rights” doctrine that would protect administrative determination of the right to enter. My guess is that even those justices don’t yet know how far they would be willing to go – or how far they can go and secure five votes of agreement. I expect this case to come down late and be sharply divided.

Correction (Nov. 15 at 6:12 p.m.): An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that “the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch” is in “Article I of the Constitution.”

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

#7675. Cutting the deadwood with Clive Cussler – my Dad

When the opportunity arose to co-write with Clive Cussler, I thought it would be a uniquely fun experience. After all, he was my father.

I knew Clive as a genial, good-natured man who loved a good laugh. He was the type of person who expected a lot from himself, but not from others. Growing up, I had ducked household chores as a kid, crashed the family car as a teen, and frittered away college tuition money on pizza and beer, all without incurring any lasting parental disdain. I expected our collaboration on adventure stories to be equally lighthearted and unruffled.

And so it was– until I submitted an early chapter in our first book together. I had written a scene in which our protagonist, Dirk Pitt, was beaten to a bloody pulp by a nefarious villain. I had crossed a line with Clive’s protagonist, and the curtain of joviality suddenly came crashing down. It was then and there that I realized the man who didn’t take life at all seriously was dead serious about his writing. Clive knew exactly how he wanted his adventure stories crafted, and he was uncompromising about their execution.

It took me back to when I was six years old, and my father began writing at night and on weekends in my childhood bedroom, which also served as the family den. He had stacks of paperback books on his desk by the likes of Hammond Innes, Donald Hamilton, and Alistair MacLean. Key passages and sections of dialogue were carefully underlined as he studied the contemporary masters of adventure writing like a Rhodes scholar.

Clive brought that same dedication to research into his own stories. He loved history, and early on began incorporating historical hooks as key elements in his books. But he never made these inclusions lightly; they were always thoroughly researched.

In the prologue to Treasure, a Roman legion is attacked by frontier barbarians in 391 A.D. The legionnaires are supported by an historically accurate contingent of Syrian archers and armed with laminated oval shields unique to that particular era of fading Roman dominance. His descriptions of the weaponry, military organization, and battle tactics demonstrated an impressive depth of study.

I was a young teen when Clive wrote his breakout bestseller, Raise the Titanic! He threw himself into researching the Titanic, borrowing every library book he could find on the ship. He joined the Titanic Historical Society to obtain its quarterly journals and enlisted me to stay up with him to watch the British production of A Night to Remember on late-night television. Such was his devotion to the topic that when he purchased and built a Revell plastic model of the ship, he manually extended the lengths of the funnels when he discovered they weren’t properly to scale. The joy he took in his research was reflected in his fictional raising of the grand ship and having it complete its maiden voyage to New York.

I share his passion for research, finding it one of the more rewarding aspects of writing. We often discussed the delicate balance involved in incorporating detailed research into a story. Knowledge of the fine details and nuances of a subject can add great flavor to a scene, but there’s also a risk of information overload. As writers, we become mini-experts on a topic and feel compelled to share our newfound knowledge. One common pitfall involves describing places we’ve visited. A writer on vacation in Dublin might later incorporate a night at a pub into a chapter scene. Eager to share the experience, she spends two pages describing the weathered wooden floor, the dusty bottles of whiskey lined above the bar, and the clover designs of the cardboard drink coasters on the tables. An atmospheric plunge suddenly turns into a boring travelogue.

Those of us who co-wrote with Clive were more than familiar with the crossed-out manuscript pages he would return to us when we got carried away with our own exuberant descriptions.

“Cut out the deadwood,” he would implore. “Make it fly.”

Clive always wanted to drive the narrative forward, but he wasn’t averse to expounding in detail at important points in the story. He might explain an ancient mystery in depth, such as the history of Troy and its related archaeological excavations in Trojan Odyssey. Or he might dive deep into describing an advanced technology incorporated into the story. These passages weren’t intended to demonstrate his knowledge, but to educate readers about elements that ultimately mattered to the plot.

Clive was a product of his time, and that also influenced his outlook on pacing and structure. Going to the movies was a ritual in his childhood, and he religiously attended matinees every Saturday afternoon. The main features were preceded by short movie serials, such as The Hurricane Express, which starred a young John Wayne. I know this because a local Denver television station aired the episodes in the 1970s, and my father watched them every week with a bowl of popcorn, as if he were eight years old again. Each episode was less than twenty minutes long, requiring a quick setup, an action sequence or two, and, of course, an ending cliffhanger. He wrote with that same sort of pacing and visual storytelling in mind. Clive especially relished ending a chapter with a cliffhanger, keeping readers eager to turn the page.

Ultimately, it was the swashbuckling sense of fun those films imparted that most influenced his approach to writing. He was more interested in entertaining readers than impressing them with his prose, and entertainment always took precedence. Clive wanted his stories to be gripping and fast-paced, of course, but the key ingredient may have been the very quality that defined his own character: a genuine sense of fun.

Dirk Cussler is the author of Clive Cussler's The Devil's Sea, and coauthor with Clive Cussler of eight previous Dirk Pitt adventures: Black Wind, Treasure of Khan, Arctic Drift, Crescent Dawn, Poseidon's Arrow, Havana Storm, Odessa Sea, and Celtic Empire. He serves as president of NUMA, where he continues his father's legacy of searching for important historical shipwrecks. He lives in Connecticut.

#7674. Former Cravath employee considers plea deal after insider trading charges

A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal. (Image from Shutterstock)

A former Cravath, Swaine & Moore employee who was arrested on charges of insider trading last week is reportedly considering a plea deal.

Federal prosecutors in New York allege that Chetram Balli, who is also known as Tony Balli, 54, accessed nonpublic information through his role as a document processing specialist for Cravath and traded ahead of at least five of the law firm’s major deals.

According to Law360, a one-page form order signed Thursday by U.S. Magistrate Judge Marcia M. Henry of the Eastern District of New York reveals that federal prosecutors and Balli are engaged in plea discussions.

The order also shows that Balli’s defense counsel requested more time to focus on negotiations without the risk of not being adequately prepared for a trial, Law360 reports.

Law360 requested but did not receive comment from either party.

Balli began working for Cravath in 1989. According to prosecutors, he supported attorneys by producing legal documents and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings and at times had access to confidential information.

Balli was arrested Thursday after prosecutors filed a criminal complaint against him and alleged that he made more than $70,000 in illicit profits.

#7672. Elly Griffiths’ 5 favorite female detectives in fiction

Women have always solved crimes. I’m sure Eve knew immediately who killed Abel, although admittedly there was only one suspect. Grendel’s mother, in Beowulf, is one of the greatest justice-seekers in literature. The Wife of Bath would make a formidable sleuth, specializing in domestic cases.

It was some time, though, before crime-solving women appeared in print. In The Female Detective by Andrew Forrester (the pseudonym of James Redding Ware), published in 1864, Mrs Gladden is thought to be a dressmaker but is, in fact, a detective. The Revelations of a Lady Detective by William Hayward, also published in 1864, features Mrs Paschall, recruited by the Chief of Police to form a squad of women officers. In Mr Bazalgette’s Agent by Leonard Merrick, published in 1888, Miriam Lea is an aristocrat who becomes a private eye after falling on hard times.

Interestingly, these first women sleuths were professionals, in that they earned their living from detection. The era of the talented but overlooked amateur, exemplified by Miss Marple, comes later.

When I created forensic archaeologist Dr Ruth Galloway, I was drawing on the tradition of the civilian expert, often a woman, who assists the police. There many great unofficial detectives in modern crime fiction;  Freida Klein in Nicki French’s books, for example, or Rhona Macleod in Lin Anderson’s series. There are also many terrific women police officers: Val McDermid’s Karen Pirie, Sarah Hilary’s Marnie Rome, Nadine Matheson’s Anjelica Henley,  Jane Casey’s Maeve Kerrigan.

Here are five of my favorite female detectives, official or otherwise.

She’s not, strictly speaking, a detective but Marian Halcombe in The Woman in White by Wilkie Collins, is surely one of the greatest sleuths in crime fiction. Laura Fairlie is ostensibly the heroine but Marian, clever, brave and intrepid, is the beating heart of the book.

The Woman in White, published in 1859/60, is known as one of the great “sensation novels” and the sweeping narrative includes abduction, organized crime and murder. One of the most thrilling scenes has Marian clambering over rooftops at night in order to overhear a conversation between the villains Percival Glyde and Count Fosco. She’s in her petticoat because her voluminous silk skirt would have rustled too much. No wonder even evil Fosco is more than half in love with her.

No list would be complete without Agatha Christie’s famous spinster sleuth. Jane Marple was apparently inspired by the many unmarried women after the first world war, who, as they grew older, were often ignored by the world around them.

Miss Marple, poised with rose clippers in her garden or bent over her crochet, makes the most of her invisibility. Almost every crime reminds Miss Marple of something she saw in her home village of St Mary Mead. She’s caustic, quietly brilliant and ruthless when on the trail of a murderer. In A Caribbean Mystery Jason Rafiel describes her as “Nemesis in a pink shawl.” Miss Marple is also surprisingly well-travelled, helped by a generous nephew and a doctor who is always happy to prescribe a holiday.

I was delighted to be asked to contribute to Marple, a new collection of short stories featuring the divine Miss M. It was a daunting task made easier by the fact that we all think we know Miss Marple but she can still always surprise us.

Ann Cleeves meant The Crow Trap to be a standalone novel. She was as surprised as anyone when, after a death at an isolated cottage in the Pennines, a rather unusual detective arrives to solve the case.

DI Vera Stanhope is “a large woman, amply covered” with a bulbous nose, man-sized feet and pitted skin. She’s scruffily dressed and carries a plastic bag containing her notes. She’s also brilliant, unconventional and frighteningly forthright. There are now thirteen Vera novels with a fourteenth, rumored to be the last, scheduled for 2027.

The TV series Vera, starring Brenda Blethyn as the eponymous detective, has run for fourteen seasons.  Through the years we have learnt more about Vera’s history and her deep connection to the Northumbrian countryside but we can never second-guess our heroine who, like the similarly disheveled Columbo, always has the last word.

Nancy Spain wrote six fantastically funny and atmospheric crime novels starring the indomitable Miriam Birdseye. I’m sure she would have gone on to write more if she hadn’t been killed in a  plane crash at the untimely age of forty-six. But in Miriam, Nancy has given us a detective for all time.

Miriam is a  wildly glamorous “vaudeville star” whose modus operandi seems to be to get engaged to the prime suspect as quickly as possible. Miriam’s sidekick is the Russian ballerina, Natasha Nevkorina, whose ambition is to do as little as possible. Miriam is always prepared to dress up in the name of detection.  Was there ever a better chapter heading than this, in Cinderella Goes to the Morgue–Enter Miriam, Disguised as a Principal Boy?

Susie Steiner also left us tragically early, dying of a brain tumor in 2022. She only wrote three novels featuring DS Manon Bradshaw but she created one of my favorite modern detectives.

Manon, named after the operatic heroine, is a terrific character: clever, kind, funny and often frustratingly stubborn. Manon’s relationships with her colleagues, Davy and Harriet, and, especially, with her adopted son, Fly, are beautifully described; full of warmth, nuance and humour. I’m sorry that there aren’t more novels about Manon, but this trilogy is crime-writing perfection.

Stella Darnell first appears in The Detective’s Daughter by Lesley Thomson. Stella is the daughter of a police officer who died before he could solve his most important case. Stella had a complicated relationship with her father and has taken another path; she’s a cleaner.

Through the course of ten intricately-plotted books, Lesley Thomson charts how Stella, reluctantly at first, becomes a private detective whilst running her own cleaning agency. She solves crimes “stain by stain.” Along the way, Stella acquires a wonderful collection of assistants, including Jack Harmon, a tube driver who can sense murder….

Elly Griffiths is the author of the Ruth Galloway and Brighton mystery series, as well as the standalone novels The Stranger Diaries, winner of the Edgar Award for Best Novel; The Postscript Murders; and Bleeding Heart Yard. She is the recipient of the CWA Dagger in the Library Award and the Mary Higgins Clark Award. She lives in Brighton, England.

#7671. Peruvian National Sentenced in Transnational Government Imposter Scheme that Defrauded Thousands of U.S. Consumers

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Carla Magaly Alcedo Mendoza (Alcedo), 45, of Lima, Peru, was sentenced today to eight years in prison and three years of supervised release for overseeing a years-long transnational fraud conspiracy that used government impersonation tactics to defraud thousands of consumers across the United States.

“The Justice Department is protecting U.S. consumers from fraudsters no matter where those fraudsters operate,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “We will continue to work with our partners at home and abroad to ensure that those who impersonate U.S. government and court officials to steal from Americans are brought to justice.”

“These criminals preyed on hardworking Americans, using fear and intimidation to steal millions of dollars. They deliberately targeted Spanish-speaking communities, impersonating government officials and threatening innocent people with arrest and legal consequences,” said Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas for the Southern District of Florida. “Today's sentence sends a clear message: no matter where you operate, if you target Americans, we will pursue you and bring you to justice.”

“Today’s sentencing of the fourteenth defendant charged in this investigation was made possible by the outstanding collaboration between Miami Division Postal Inspectors, the Justice Department, and our international partners,” said Inspector in Charge Bladismir Rojo of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Miami Division. “Transnational criminal organizations who victimize our citizens are not beyond our reach.”

According to court documents, Alcedo was the operator of a Peruvian call center that defrauded and extorted U.S. residents by falsely threatening them with arrest, court proceedings, and immigration consequences. Alcedo admitted that she owned and operated a call center in Lima, Peru, that placed unsolicited calls to Spanish-speaking consumers in the United States and falsely claimed that they had won or qualified for free products, including computer tablets and English language courses. On later calls, Alcedo and her co-conspirators falsely claimed that victims were contractually obligated to pay large sums of money to receive the products. Alcedo and her co-conspirators impersonated government officials and lawyers to intimidate victims and force them to pay. Alcedo and her co-conspirators also threatened victims with court proceedings, arrest, and other legal consequences if they did not pay. The scheme spanned several years and thousands of victims made payments to Alcedo. Collectively, the scheme was responsible for defrauding more than 30,000 Spanish-speaking residents of the United States out of $15 million.

Alcedo was extradited from Peru in April 2025 and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud in August 2026.

Including today’s sentencing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, 14 defendants have now been convicted and sentenced in connection with this scheme. The 14 defendants include 10 Peruvian call center owner-operators and four distribution center owner-operators who processed payments, distributed products, and facilitated the fraud in the United States, and a telephone service provider who facilitated the fraud schemes across the call centers in Peru. Alcedo and many of the defendants shared strategies on how to defraud consumer victims across the United States.

Alcedo is the 10th defendant charged in this scheme to be extradited from Peru and sentenced in federal court. In 2021 and 2022, Henrry Milla, Carlos Espinoza, Jerson Renteria, Fernan Huerta, Omar Cuzcano, Evelyng Milla, and Josmell Espinoza received sentences ranging from 88 months to 110 months in prison. In 2024, Jose Alejandro Zuñiga Cano was sentenced to 98 months in prison.

Criminal Division Senior Trial Attorney and Transnational Criminal Litigation Coordinator Phil Toomajian prosecuted the case and Assistant U.S. Attorney Annika Miranda for the Southern District of Florida is handling asset forfeiture. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida, State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service, U.S. Marshals Service, Peruvian National Prosecutor General’s Office, and Peruvian National Police provided critical assistance with the case and extradition.

This case is part of efforts being undertaken by the Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Cyber-Enabled Scam Initiative (CSI). The CSI is a dedicated team of prosecutors built to find scammers who prey on Americans, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. CSI brings together expert prosecutors from across the Criminal Division to accelerate the prosecution of cyber-enabled financial crimes, including complex frauds, government imposter schemes, romance and inheritance scams, financially motivated sextortion, lottery and sweepstakes scams, and other predatory schemes. With nationwide jurisdiction and global reach, CSI leverages every available tool to dismantle criminal operations, pursue bad actors, recover criminal proceeds, and obtain justice for victims. The Criminal Division partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country and is a founding member of the Scam Center Strike Force.

#7670. What Trump cases might soon return to the Supreme Court?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

During the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats on two of his signature initiatives – his efforts to limit birthright citizenship and impose sweeping tariffs – as well as his initial attempt to fire Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those issues. In the wake of the court’s decisions in each of the three cases, Trump continues to fight on, which has led (or could lead) to litigation that may reach the court again.

The Democratic Party’s decisive victory in the midterm elections, which gave it a majority in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, could theoretically hinder Trump’s plans. However, Democrats would need not just a majority to pass legislation curbing the president’s authority but a veto-proof majority: 67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House, which could be more difficult to obtain.

#7668. Christina Henry on translating the unexpected horrors of motherhood into fiction

We all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like. Society creates expectations for mothers, and mothers who color outside those lines are often censured by those around them.

But being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard. If you carry a child you might think that pregnancy will be nine months of glowing, radiant bliss (that’s what all those parenting influencers say on TikTok, don’t they?) Instead, you’re coping with swollen feet and sciatica, and the constant worry that you might do something that will accidentally harm your growing baby.

Once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out. But parenting isn’t just drippy ice cream cones on the beach and smiling while riding carousels. There are so many things you can’t anticipate—unexpected illnesses, trouble at school, headstrong kids who simply want their own way.

The truth of the matter that having a child and raising a child are often some of the most anxiety-riddled years of a person’s life. Even when nothing’s going wrong, a mother can often feel like something just might go wrong. The worry they are feeling is somehow a hedge against bad things happening—parental anxiety as a shield against actual harm.

Fictional mothers, of course, get the worst of it. It’s bad enough that real-world mothers have to cope with spiking fevers and school permission forms and judgmental in-laws. But what if you desperately want a child but it turns out your baby was also, say, the son of Satan? Or what if you love your children with all your heart but you keep hearing things, seeing things that you aren’t sure are actually there? What if the people around you aren’t to be trusted? What if you feel like you can’t trust yourself?

Everyone knows about Rosemary, right? Poor Rosemary Woodhouse, whose gaslighting jerk of a husband, Guy, trades her womb for a successful career.

In Ira Levin’s classic novel of motherhood horror, Rosemary’s Baby, Rosemary is a cheery newlywed who wants to have a child. Guy is a struggling actor who keeps just missing his big break and wants to wait a little longer to start a family. A bit of timely luck allows them to sign a lease in an older building called the Bramford, a place that’s notoriously difficult to get into. Rosemary is thrilled that, at least, she will have the decoration of a new place to keep her busy, but she still wishes for a baby.

An older couple, Roman and Minnie Castavet, live in the next apartment. Rosemary finds them nosy and annoying, but for some reason Guy likes them and starts to visit regularly. Then, a miracle happens. The actor who cast in a role that Guy almost got is suddenly struck blind (a miracle for Guy, of course, not so much for the other actor) and Guy lands a role that can make his career.  Soon after this unexpectedly fortuitous occurrence, he decides that he does, in fact, want a baby.

Shortly after, Rosemary has a terrible dream—a dream about a beast who rapes her while several people look on. And then, the second miracle happens. Rosemary is pregnant. Except her pregnancy doesn’t feel right, and everyone around her keeps telling her it’s fine.

Rosemary’s journey is so harrowing because no matter what she says or does or even knows with absolute certainty, no one will believe her. If you’ve never read this one it’s time to give it a try.

Kit Burgoyne’s The Captive is a clever play on the I’ve-been-impregnated-by-Satan-against-my-will story, or in this case, by an entity alternately referred to as “The Long-Before” or “Him.” An underground revolutionary group that call themselves the Nail decide to kidnap Adeline Woolsaw, the wealthy heiress of a vast network of connected businesses, in hopes of exposing the Woolsaws and their corruption to the public. The only time Adeline ever seems to leave the vast estate where she lives is to go to the doctor’s office, so the group decides to grab her as she leaves her appointment.

Unfortunately for the Nail, Adeline is pregnant. Even more unfortunately, Adeline is going into labor in the van. Just to add to their confusion, Adeline most definitely does not want to return home to her parents. It seems that her parents worship this evil entity and arranged to have Adeline carry His child in order to establish total world domination.

This pitch-black story skewers the cultists, the radical revolutionaries and the oligarchs that run everything equally and mashes it all up into a super-fun (and frequently gory) thriller.

Helen Phillip’s The Need is probably one of my favorite novels of the last ten years. I’ve never read another book that so accurately embodies both the intense love of a mother for her children and also the profound, dragging monotony of the daily tasks that make up her day.

Molly is a mom of two and a paleobotanist, alone with the kids while her partner travels. She is exhausted, exhausted in that bone-deep way parents often are, feeling like she wants to stay on top of everything but she simply cannot.

When she hears footsteps in her home she thinks she’s imagining them. She’s anxious about a potential home invasion. She can’t trust herself. She’s just sleep-deprived. But then she comes face to face with an intruder wearing a mask, and the reality of Molly’s world tilts precariously on its side.

The less you know about this one, the better. It unfolds like a strange and fascinating puzzle box, revealing layers as it goes.

Neena Viel’s debut Listen to Your Sister isn’t about a mother, per se. But it is about Calla Williams, a twenty-five-year-old woman just trying to keep it together, who reluctantly agrees to become the guardian to her sixteen-year-old brother Jamie. Jamie, like most 16-year-olds, is not interested in his sister’s authority, or any kind of authority, really. Their brother Dre agreed to help Calla with Jamie, but he has his own struggles and isn’t exactly present.

Calla keeps trying, keeps sacrificing, keeps muddling along trying to do her best like every mother figure.  Ever since her brothers were young she’s had visions of their dying in horrible ways, and her nightmares stoke her anxiety over their well-being. But her resentment is growing. No matter how much she loves her brothers, they don’t seem to love her enough to change.

One day Jamie’s behavior goes a little too far and the siblings are forced to flee their homes to hide out at a cabin in the woods. It’s there that Calla’s patience finally snaps, and her brothers discover that the nightmares Calla has had all their lives might just be real.

Neena Viel’s writing is so intense, so profoundly visual, that this book has been indelibly imprinted on my brain. I’m still thinking about it months later.

In my own upcoming novel Pinfeathers, stay-at-home mom Nora Pacetti is tired and frustrated that her husband, Adam, isn’t keeping up his end of the parenting bargain. But those problems seem trivial once Nora discovers a strange object sticking out of her baby’s arm.

Nora thinks it must be a splinter. But when she examines it closely the object seems to have come through her daughter’s skin, not pierced it from the outside. Then Nora’s mother Giulia looks at it and renders her verdict—it’s a pinfeather, a baby feather.

Nora doesn’t know what to believe, and then she finds another one. Does her daughter have a strange disease, or is she actually turning into a bird?

Christina Henry is the author of The Mermaid, Lost Boy, Alice, Red Queen, and the national bestselling Black Wings series featuring Agent of Death Madeline Black and her popcorn-loving gargoyle, Beezle.
